sources.title: Google’s SynthID AI content detector expands globally, will work on Apple’s models ‘soon’ - 9to5Google
passages: Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models.
But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.
Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future.
The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection.
According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.
So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple.

That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.
Stay up to date on news from Google headquarters…

extraction.body: Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners. SynthID is a necessary tool as AI content has taken hold of heavy portions of the internet. Models have evolved so much that it’s nearly impossible to tell whether some videos or photos are even real, and it has you second-guessing whether real ones are generated. SynthID takes aim at that problem by introducing invisible watermarks at the generation stage, and when used on an image, it will detect those watermarks. Of course, that only works if the image generation tool inserts its own footprint to begin with. Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future. The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection. According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility. The new SynthID will work with content generated on Google’s own Gemini, a given, as well as content from more partners. So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple. That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together. extraction.body: SynthID Detector — a new portal to help identify AI-generated content The SynthID Detector can help determine if an image created using Google AI contains a SynthID watermark. VP, Science and Strategic Initiatives, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Advances in generative AI are making it possible for people to create content in entirely new ways — from text to high quality audio, images and videos. As these capabilities advance and become more broadly available, questions of authenticity, context and verification emerge. Today we’re announcing SynthID Detector, a verification portal to quickly and efficiently identify AI-generated content made with Google AI. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media. It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID. When we launched SynthID — a state-of-the-art tool that embeds imperceptible watermarks and enables the identification of AI-generated content — our aim was to provide a suite of novel technical solutions to help minimise misinformation and misattribution. SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations. While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google. Over 10 billion pieces of content have already been watermarked with SynthID. When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark. If a watermark is detected, the portal will highlight specific portions of the content most likely to be watermarked. For audio, the portal pinpoints specific segments where a SynthID watermark is detected, and for images, it indicates areas where a watermark is most likely. We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly. Journalists, media professionals and researchers can join our waitlist to gain access to the SynthID Detector. To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models. And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com . This means that more content across the web has SynthID embedded in it, not just content generated by Google. At the same time, it’s important that other partners will be able to detect when a piece of content has been watermarked with SynthID. That’s why today we’re also announcing our partnership with GetReal Security , the world’s leading content verification platform. Content transparency remains a complex challenge. To continue to inform and empower people engaging with AI-generated content, we believe it’s vital to continue collaborating with the AI community and broaden access to transparency tools. The author would like to thank Miguel de Andrés-Clavera and the Google Partner Innovation team for their assistance in developing the SynthID Detector portal. Product in development; final product details may differ. Video and text watermark detection will be rolled out in the coming weeks.

sources.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
passages: Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic .
SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.
It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though.
Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.
You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts.
While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it.
Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.”
Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools.
The website will have a disclaimer saying as much.
It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio.
This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually.
Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.
The previous detection tools had a similar limit.
Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools.
The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar.
This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow.
Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that.

extraction.body: The new SynthID website can now identify AI content from Google, OpenAI, and more. Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website. SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.” Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem. Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media. You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts. While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it. Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.” The previous detection tools had a similar limit. Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools. The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar. This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow. Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools. However, Google’s partners are far from the only sources of AI content. Some model providers use different watermarking tech (like Meta), while others use no watermarks at all. And then there are open-weight models that people can run on their own hardware to produce increasingly realistic AI content that doesn’t even include simple metadata labeling. That means there is plenty of AI content that will not be identified as AI in the SynthID tool. The website will have a disclaimer saying as much. It’s also plausible that despite Google’s efforts, someone will find a way to remove SynthID, making existing AI content look more legit. It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate. The best approach might be the opposite—using cryptographic technologies like C2PA to label real images, video, and audio as they are created. Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that. In the meantime, SynthID is the best bet you’ve got to identify AI fakes. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.

Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.

extraction.body: The new SynthID website can now identify AI content from Google, OpenAI, and more. Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website. SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.” Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem. Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media. You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts. While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it. Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.” The previous detection tools had a similar limit. Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools. The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar. This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow. Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools. However, Google’s partners are far from the only sources of AI content. Some model providers use different watermarking tech (like Meta), while others use no watermarks at all. And then there are open-weight models that people can run on their own hardware to produce increasingly realistic AI content that doesn’t even include simple metadata labeling. That means there is plenty of AI content that will not be identified as AI in the SynthID tool. The website will have a disclaimer saying as much. It’s also plausible that despite Google’s efforts, someone will find a way to remove SynthID, making existing AI content look more legit. It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate. The best approach might be the opposite—using cryptographic technologies like C2PA to label real images, video, and audio as they are created. Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that. In the meantime, SynthID is the best bet you’ve got to identify AI fakes. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

Microsoft ( MSFT ) unveiled its Nvidia ( NVDA )-powered Surface Laptop Ultra during an event in San Francisco, Calif., on Wednesday. Designed to compete with Apple's ( AAPL ) MacBook Pro laptops for AI, video workloads, and gaming, the $2,599 Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most powerful Surface to date, thanks to its Arm ( ARM )-based Nvidia RTX Spark processor. Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices, Pavan Davuluri, said the chip features up to a staggering 128GB of unified memory, giving it the ability to run demanding AI models that other laptops can't. According to Tom Mainelli, IDC's group vice president of device and consumer research, the Surface Laptop Ultra will likely appeal to early adopters across both the consumer and enterprise spaces. "Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance. "But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers." Orchestration is the process of determining which AI models and agents to use, when, and for what purpose. For instance, you wouldn't want to use an expensive cloud-based model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to perform a task that a free, local model installed on your PC can handle. During Wednesday's event, Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices explained that the company is bringing hybrid AI capabilities and AI agent security to Windows via a series of updates. The enterprise and consumer tech industries have been leaning heavily into local AI models as an alternative to cloud-based models and agents. Kicking off a new arms race in the laptop and desktop space. Microsoft demonstrated the Surface Laptop Ultra's performance in a video clip showing it running the video game "Gears of War: E Day," GitHub Copilot, and the video editing platform DaVinci Resolve at the same time, something that would chew up a standard laptop. When it comes to AI specifically, Microsoft says the Surface Laptop Ultra offers 4.3x faster AI image generation than a MacBook Pro with Apple's M5 Pro chip and 6.2x faster video generation. The PC industry, like the rest of the tech sector, is contending with the ongoing shortage of memory and storage chips. That's forced companies to raise the prices of their devices, cutting into overall sales. But, so far, those increased prices have helped insulate device makers from the worst of the sales declines. "Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance. "But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers."

Orchestration is the process of determining which AI models and agents to use, when, and for what purpose. For instance, you wouldn't want to use an expensive cloud-based model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to perform a task that a free, local model installed on your PC can handle.

During Wednesday's event, Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices explained that the company is bringing hybrid AI capabilities and AI agent security to Windows via a series of updates.

The enterprise and consumer tech industries have been leaning heavily into local AI models as an alternative to cloud-based models and agents. Kicking off a new arms race in the laptop and desktop space.

When it comes to AI specifically, Microsoft says the Surface Laptop Ultra offers 4.3x faster AI image generation than a MacBook Pro with Apple's M5 Pro chip and 6.2x faster video generation.

The PC industry, like the rest of the tech sector, is contending with the ongoing shortage of memory and storage chips. That's forced companies to raise the prices of their devices, cutting into overall sales.
But, so far, those increased prices have helped insulate device makers from the worst of the sales declines.

It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least. This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 . Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive. Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here . NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops. The Surface Laptop Ultra, which was announced in June , is one of the first devices powered by RTX Spark, and from the brief glimpse we got earlier this year, it appears to be a direct competitor to Apple's powerful MacBook Pro. It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want. But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch). Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. To recap, the NVIDIA RTX Spark will feature 6,144 Blackwell GPU cores, 20 Arm CPU cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power. I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra. Aside from being one of the first systems with RTX Spark, it just seems to be another premium laptop. But I'm hoping to discover what inspired this poetic take on the notebook from Microsoft Corporate Vice President Brett Ostrum: "A machine like this should not sit still. It should be pushed. Taken to the edge. Used to make real what others call impossible. It belongs in the hands of world makers." Microsoft isn't really keeping this a secret: The company wants us to know it's going to have some big agentic AI news next week. That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw . Much like it did with Recall, Microsoft could easily run into unforeseen privacy issues with a true AI agent, which would potentially be able to see all of your files, your browsing history and act on your behalf. We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge. However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality. The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs . The core idea of agentic AI — letting an AI tool work on tasks with minimal input — sounds intriguing, especially to people who've already fully changed their workflows around modern AI models. But it's also not something that will easily translate to people outside of the tech world. I can see why so many programmers got excited about OpenClaw , but only a few people will want to manage an agent with an archaic command line interface.

extraction.body: Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time. On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.) Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7. The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them. Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event. Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.” He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.” The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley. Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises. Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800. coreStoryFacts.text: Microsoft ( MSFT ) unveiled its Nvidia ( NVDA )-powered Surface Laptop Ultra during an event in San Francisco, Calif., on Wednesday.

Designed to compete with Apple's ( AAPL ) MacBook Pro laptops for AI, video workloads, and gaming, the $2,599 Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most powerful Surface to date, thanks to its Arm ( ARM )-based Nvidia RTX Spark processor.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
"Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance.
"But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers."

Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices, Pavan Davuluri, said the chip features up to a staggering 128GB of unified memory, giving it the ability to run demanding AI models that other laptops can't.
It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least.
This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 .

Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive.
We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here .
We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge.
However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality.
The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs .
NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops.
It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want.
That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw .
I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra.
Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says.
That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.

Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.
Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday.
Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC.
It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800.

Microsoft ( MSFT ) unveiled its Nvidia ( NVDA )-powered Surface Laptop Ultra during an event in San Francisco, Calif., on Wednesday. Designed to compete with Apple's ( AAPL ) MacBook Pro laptops for AI, video workloads, and gaming, the $2,599 Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most powerful Surface to date, thanks to its Arm ( ARM )-based Nvidia RTX Spark processor. Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices, Pavan Davuluri, said the chip features up to a staggering 128GB of unified memory, giving it the ability to run demanding AI models that other laptops can't. According to Tom Mainelli, IDC's group vice president of device and consumer research, the Surface Laptop Ultra will likely appeal to early adopters across both the consumer and enterprise spaces. "Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance. "But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers." Orchestration is the process of determining which AI models and agents to use, when, and for what purpose. For instance, you wouldn't want to use an expensive cloud-based model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to perform a task that a free, local model installed on your PC can handle. During Wednesday's event, Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices explained that the company is bringing hybrid AI capabilities and AI agent security to Windows via a series of updates. The enterprise and consumer tech industries have been leaning heavily into local AI models as an alternative to cloud-based models and agents. Kicking off a new arms race in the laptop and desktop space. Microsoft demonstrated the Surface Laptop Ultra's performance in a video clip showing it running the video game "Gears of War: E Day," GitHub Copilot, and the video editing platform DaVinci Resolve at the same time, something that would chew up a standard laptop. When it comes to AI specifically, Microsoft says the Surface Laptop Ultra offers 4.3x faster AI image generation than a MacBook Pro with Apple's M5 Pro chip and 6.2x faster video generation. The PC industry, like the rest of the tech sector, is contending with the ongoing shortage of memory and storage chips. That's forced companies to raise the prices of their devices, cutting into overall sales. But, so far, those increased prices have helped insulate device makers from the worst of the sales declines. extraction.body: Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time. On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.) Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7. The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them. Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event. Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.” He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.” The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley. Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises. Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800. passages: SpaceX may have a larger opportunity in the long-run.
But for 2027 specifically, Nvidia is my better stock to buy.
The reason isn't that SpaceX lacks meaningful catalysts.
SpaceX is simultaneously scaling Starlink, building AI data centers, developing Starship, expanding government operations, and pursuing space-based infrastructure.
If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.
While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see.
For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup.
SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027.
On one side is Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), the company that essentially supplies the picks and shovels of the AI boom.

On the other is Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), which has evolved from a rocket company into a vertically integrated technology platform spanning Starlink, AI infrastructure, government contracting, and space exploration.
The biggest catalyst for Nvidia stock in 2027 is the transition from the Blackwell chip architecture to the Vera Rubin platform.
Management says the platform is already ramping into full production, with systems running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave , and Nebius .
For the third quarter, Nvidia's server CPU ecosystem, which includes Rubin, is expected to generate $20 billion in revenue and is on pace to more than double by next year.
The interesting part of this forecast is that it does not assume any compute revenue from China.
This highlights one of Nvidia's biggest potential catalysts for 2027.
If China becomes a meaningful market again, Nvidia could have upside that isn't currently reflected in its guidance.
SpaceX enters 2027 from a much different position.
In the second quarter, the company's revenue nearly doubled to $7.8 billion.
Growth was primarily fueled by Starlink and AI infrastructure.
SpaceX says its combined businesses are on track to reach $100 billion in annualized run-rate revenue by the end of the year.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

In addition, management recently disclosed two other cloud hosting agreements expected to contribute roughly $1.11 billion of monthly revenue beginning in December as well as another six-month, $6.7 billion capacity deal.
As usual, the data center segment was the star of the show -- generating $89 billion of revenue and soaring 117% year over year.
Management guided third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.
Smart investors understand that spectacular growth doesn't necessarily guarantee a stock will rise if enormous capital outlays are required.
Nvidia's recently expanded share repurchase program also gives it another quiet advantage.
The company now has $235 billion remaining under its authorization, providing significant firepower to buy back stock through next year.
When combined with an attractive valuation profile, Nvidia is hard to pass up.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Nvidia wasn't one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

But if I had to choose only one for next year, I think the answer comes down to a surprisingly simple idea: which company has the more predictable path to turning AI spending into profits?
There are risks when it comes to buying Nvidia stock.
Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are developing custom AI chips.
Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices continues to win deals with hyperscalers as it tries to take market share in the GPU and CPU landscapes.
At a macro level, Nvidia will also need AI infrastructure spending to remain elevated.
Nvidia offers something I value more over the next year: visibility.
For Nvidia, AI spending is already translating into enormous revenue, high gross margins, and substantial cash generation.
Rubin provides a new product cycle heading into next year, while unrelenting demand from hyperscalers, frontier labs, sovereign governments, and enterprises continues expanding.

If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road. While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see. For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup. SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027. The biggest catalyst for Nvidia stock in 2027 is the transition from the Blackwell chip architecture to the Vera Rubin platform. Management says the platform is already ramping into full production, with systems running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave , and Nebius . For the third quarter, Nvidia's server CPU ecosystem, which includes Rubin, is expected to generate $20 billion in revenue and is on pace to more than double by next year. Investors looking for ways to profit from artificial intelligence (AI) have an interesting choice heading into 2027. On one side is Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), the company that essentially supplies the picks and shovels of the AI boom. On the other is Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), which has evolved from a rocket company into a vertically integrated technology platform spanning Starlink, AI infrastructure, government contracting, and space exploration.

Both companies have enormous catalysts heading into 2027 and each stock comes with expectations that leave little room for disappointment. But if I had to choose only one for next year, I think the answer comes down to a surprisingly simple idea: which company has the more predictable path to turning AI spending into profits?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The biggest catalyst for Nvidia stock in 2027 is the transition from the Blackwell chip architecture to the Vera Rubin platform. Rubin isn't some distant product roadmap. Management says the platform is already ramping into full production, with systems running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave , and Nebius . For the third quarter, Nvidia's server CPU ecosystem, which includes Rubin, is expected to generate $20 billion in revenue and is on pace to more than double by next year.

Rubin is arriving while Nvidia's existing businesses are still growing at a staggering pace. During the second quarter, the company's revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. As usual, the data center segment was the star of the show -- generating $89 billion of revenue and soaring 117% year over year. Management guided third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.

The interesting part of this forecast is that it does not assume any compute revenue from China. This highlights one of Nvidia's biggest potential catalysts for 2027. If China becomes a meaningful market again, Nvidia could have upside that isn't currently reflected in its guidance.

There are risks when it comes to buying Nvidia stock. Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are developing custom AI chips. Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices continues to win deals with hyperscalers as it tries to take market share in the GPU and CPU landscapes. At a macro level, Nvidia will also need AI infrastructure spending to remain elevated.
SpaceX enters 2027 from a much different position. In the second quarter, the company's revenue nearly doubled to $7.8 billion. Growth was primarily fueled by Starlink and AI infrastructure.

SpaceX has signed billions of dollars of AI compute agreements with Anthropic, Google, and Reflection AI. In addition, management recently disclosed two other cloud hosting agreements expected to contribute roughly $1.11 billion of monthly revenue beginning in December as well as another six-month, $6.7 billion capacity deal.

SpaceX says its combined businesses are on track to reach $100 billion in annualized run-rate revenue by the end of the year. Management also expects cumulative compute capacity to approach 10 gigawatts by the end of 2027, underscoring the importance of AI to the growth narrative.

This creates an interesting flywheel. At scale, SpaceX can generate cash from Starlink and its launch cadence and reinvest into AI infrastructure. In the long-run, the company can use Starship to deploy next-generation communications and compute infrastructure into orbit. Taken together, SpaceX believes its rockets, connectivity, and AI infrastructure create a $28.5 trillion addressable market.

The problem is cost. SpaceX spent $18.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex) during the second quarter alone and remains free cash flow negative. Smart investors understand that spectacular growth doesn't necessarily guarantee a stock will rise if enormous capital outlays are required.

SpaceX may have a larger opportunity in the long-run. But for 2027 specifically, Nvidia is my better stock to buy. The reason isn't that SpaceX lacks meaningful catalysts. In fact, it's almost the opposite. SpaceX is simultaneously scaling Starlink, building AI data centers, developing Starship, expanding government operations, and pursuing space-based infrastructure. If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.

Nvidia offers something I value more over the next year: visibility. For Nvidia, AI spending is already translating into enormous revenue, high gross margins, and substantial cash generation. Rubin provides a new product cycle heading into next year, while unrelenting demand from hyperscalers, frontier labs, sovereign governments, and enterprises continues expanding.

Nvidia's recently expanded share repurchase program also gives it another quiet advantage. The company now has $235 billion remaining under its authorization, providing significant firepower to buy back stock through next year. When combined with an attractive valuation profile, Nvidia is hard to pass up.

While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see. When I'm choosing between two growth stocks, I'd rather own the company where secular tailwinds are already producing recurring profits than the one still spending aggressively to build its next engine. For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup. SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027.

passages: Investors looking for ways to profit from artificial intelligence (AI) have an interesting choice heading into 2027. On one side is Nvidia ( NVDA -0.74% ) , the company that essentially supplies the picks and shovels of the AI boom. On the other is Space Exploration Technologies ( SPCX -2.51% ) , which has evolved from a rocket company into a vertically integrated technology platform spanning Starlink, AI infrastructure, government contracting, and space exploration.

Both companies have enormous catalysts heading into 2027 and each stock comes with expectations that leave little room for disappointment. But if I had to choose only one for next year, I think the answer comes down to a surprisingly simple idea: which company has the more predictable path to turning AI spending into profits?

The biggest catalyst for Nvidia stock in 2027 is the transition from the Blackwell chip architecture to the Vera Rubin platform. Rubin isn't some distant product roadmap. Management says the platform is already ramping into full production, with systems running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave , and Nebius . For the third quarter, Nvidia's server CPU ecosystem, which includes Rubin, is expected to generate $20 billion in revenue and is on pace to more than double by next year.

Rubin is arriving while Nvidia's existing businesses are still growing at a staggering pace. During the second quarter, the company's revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. As usual, the data center segment was the star of the show -- generating $89 billion of revenue and soaring 117% year over year. Management guided third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.

The interesting part of this forecast is that it does not assume any compute revenue from China . This highlights one of Nvidia's biggest potential catalysts for 2027. If China becomes a meaningful market again, Nvidia could have upside that isn't currently reflected in its guidance.

There are risks when it comes to buying Nvidia stock. Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are developing custom AI chips. Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices continues to win deals with hyperscalers as it tries to take market share in the GPU and CPU landscapes. At a macro level, Nvidia will also need AI infrastructure spending to remain elevated.
SpaceX enters 2027 from a much different position. In the second quarter, the company's revenue nearly doubled to $7.8 billion. Growth was primarily fueled by Starlink and AI infrastructure.

SpaceX has signed billions of dollars of AI compute agreements with Anthropic, Google, and Reflection AI. In addition, management recently disclosed two other cloud hosting agreements expected to contribute roughly $1.11 billion of monthly revenue beginning in December as well as another six-month, $6.7 billion capacity deal.

SpaceX says its combined businesses are on track to reach $100 billion in annualized run-rate revenue by the end of the year. Management also expects cumulative compute capacity to approach 10 gigawatts by the end of 2027, underscoring the importance of AI to the growth narrative.

This creates an interesting flywheel. At scale, SpaceX can generate cash from Starlink and its launch cadence and reinvest into AI infrastructure. In the long-run, the company can use Starship to deploy next-generation communications and compute infrastructure into orbit. Taken together, SpaceX believes its rockets, connectivity, and AI infrastructure create a $28.5 trillion addressable market .

The problem is cost. SpaceX spent $18.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex) during the second quarter alone and remains free cash flow negative. Smart investors understand that spectacular growth doesn't necessarily guarantee a stock will rise if enormous capital outlays are required.

SpaceX may have a larger opportunity in the long-run. But for 2027 specifically, Nvidia is my better stock to buy. The reason isn't that SpaceX lacks meaningful catalysts. In fact, it's almost the opposite. SpaceX is simultaneously scaling Starlink, building AI data centers, developing Starship, expanding government operations, and pursuing space-based infrastructure. If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.

Nvidia offers something I value more over the next year: visibility . For Nvidia, AI spending is already translating into enormous revenue, high gross margins, and substantial cash generation. Rubin provides a new product cycle heading into next year, while unrelenting demand from hyperscalers, frontier labs, sovereign governments , and enterprises continues expanding.

Nvidia's recently expanded share repurchase program also gives it another quiet advantage. The company now has $235 billion remaining under its authorization , providing significant firepower to buy back stock through next year. When combined with an attractive valuation profile , Nvidia is hard to pass up.

While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see. When I'm choosing between two growth stocks, I'd rather own the company where secular tailwinds are already producing recurring profits than the one still spending aggressively to build its next engine. For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup. SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027.

Both companies have enormous catalysts heading into 2027 and each stock comes with expectations that leave little room for disappointment. But if I had to choose only one for next year, I think the answer comes down to a surprisingly simple idea: which company has the more predictable path to turning AI spending into profits?

sources.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
passages: At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text.
It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached. Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said. Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text. The new experience will be available starting this fall on Windows 11 PCs, according to Windows and Surface boss Pavan Davuluri.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

Microsoft announced the Surface Laptop Ultra at the event, a machine equipped with Nvidia RTX Spark silicon aimed at improved AI performance.
Microsoft has also emphasized agent workspaces and user-controlled settings, designs intended to keep privacy and security in the foreground.

We’re introducing agents in Microsoft 365 designed to help scale individual impact and transform business processes.
These new agents complement the autonomous agents that we announced in October 2024 for sales, service, finance, and supply chain professionals—and we’re just getting started.
We’ll create many more agents in the coming year that will give customers the competitive advantage they need to future-proof their organization.
September 23 3 min read Building the system for AI at work There’s no shortage of sound and fury in AI right now.
Visit Microsoft365.com/copilot or download the Microsoft 365 app on your mobile device.
To empower every IT team to lead at scale, we’re introducing the Copilot Control System —designed for IT to confidently adopt and accelerate the business value of Copilot and agents.
Microsoft 365 Copilot is becoming a daily habit for people around the world—already, nearly 70% of Fortune 500 companies are using it.

Dow anticipates that Copilot will save it millions of dollars on shipping operations in the first year; at Bank of Queensland Group , 70% of users are saving two and a half to five hours per week; Eaton is speeding up internal documentation processes by 83%; and Accenture is going big, rolling out Copilot to 100,000 employees.

1 Blind, side-by-side human intelligence tasks conducted on behalf of Microsoft in July and August 2024, each with 9 participants (judges) to compare user satisfaction with query responses of Microsoft Copilot and a competitor.

Microsoft 365 Copilot is becoming a daily habit for people around the world—already, nearly 70% of Fortune 500 companies are using it. Dow anticipates that Copilot will save it millions of dollars on shipping operations in the first year; at Bank of Queensland Group , 70% of users are saving two and a half to five hours per week; Eaton is speeding up internal documentation processes by 83%; and Accenture is going big, rolling out Copilot to 100,000 employees.

Today at Microsoft Ignite 2024 , we’re accelerating our ambition to empower every employee with Copilot as a personal assistant and to transform every business process with agents built in Microsoft Copilot Studio.
These announcements build on our wave 2 momentum, including the new autonomous agent capabilities that we announced in October 2024 .

Thanks to our customers, we have the world’s best feedback loop on AI at work. We’ve dramatically improved Copilot performance—responses are two times faster on average and response satisfaction is nearly three times higher 1 —and shipped hundreds of new features. And we’re adding new value to Copilot to tackle work’s biggest pain points and help every employee scale their impact—from automating repetitive tasks to managing your calendar.

Copilot is where you interact with agents , and Copilot Studio is where you can easily create, manage, and connect agents to Copilot. We’re introducing agents in Microsoft 365 designed to help scale individual impact and transform business processes. These new agents complement the autonomous agents that we announced in October 2024 for sales, service, finance, and supply chain professionals—and we’re just getting started. We’ll create many more agents in the coming year that will give customers the competitive advantage they need to future-proof their organization.

Chief information officers and IT professionals are at the epicenter of AI transformation. To empower every IT team to lead at scale, we’re introducing the Copilot Control System —designed for IT to confidently adopt and accelerate the business value of Copilot and agents.

In today’s digital landscape, protecting your organization’s data from emerging threats and ensuring system integrity is paramount. We’re pushing the boundaries to continue making Windows the most secure and performant platform for you and your organization.

To empower every employee with Copilot as a personal assistant and transform every business process with agents built in Copilot Studio, start using Copilot today. Visit Microsoft365.com/copilot or download the Microsoft 365 app on your mobile device.

sources.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
passages: At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text.
It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch. He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes. In the demo, Andreou told Microsoft’s Autopilot tool that he had received an email from his accountant. He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. In 2025, Microsoft put Copilot Actions into experimental preview for Windows Insiders, the company’s early-access testing group, with features covering local file operations and local file search. Andreou’s own trajectory tracks with it: he was promoted to EVP of Copilot in March 2026, taking charge of both consumer and commercial initiatives. AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user. Microsoft has also emphasized agent workspaces and user-controlled settings, designs intended to keep privacy and security in the foreground. Microsoft is leaning on the one asset its AI competitors cannot easily copy: ownership of the operating system that a huge share of the world’s PCs run on. OpenAI and Anthropic build powerful models, but they generally reach users through apps and interfaces layered on top of someone else’s platform. Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work. The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features. The opt-in design means adoption depends entirely on users actively choosing to grant access, rather than discovering the feature by default. For enterprises, restricted folder access plus separate agent accounts give IT departments something concrete to evaluate instead of a promise. sources.title: Microsoft's Hybrid Intelligence gives Copilot more control over your files
passages: Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent.
For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways.
Microsoft has unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, a set of software orchestration tools that will let your PC run AI models locally.
Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios.
This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.
It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech.

sources.title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90 - The Guardian
passages: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft.
When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom

Margaret Hamilton, the MIT computer scientist who led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept. 30. She was 90. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, first at the Instrumentation Lab and later at Lincoln Laboratory. She authored more than 130 publications and helped establish software engineering as a dedicated field. In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history," the White House citation read. "Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics at the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a bachelor's degree in 1958. She moved to Boston in 1959 and found a temporary position in MIT's meteorology department, working with professor Edward N. Lorenz on weather prediction software. That work later informed Lorenz's pioneering research on chaos theory. In 1961, Hamilton joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory as a programmer on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system. She wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer, which the U.S. Air Force used to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this period, she became interested in software reliability, a concept that was largely unexplored at the time. In 1965, Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw a newspaper advertisement: MIT's Instrumentation Lab was seeking programmers to develop software to send a man to the moon. NASA had awarded the lab the contract to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Hamilton applied and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, and the first female programmer on the project. She initially worked on software for uncrewed Apollo missions, then moved up to lead the team developing onboard flight software for crewed missions. By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, overseeing more than 400 people. "There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. "Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers." Hamilton's approach to software development proved critical during the Apollo missions. One incident, known as "the Lauren error," occurred when her four-year-old daughter Lauren accidentally activated a pre-launch program called P01 while playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab, crashing the simulator midflight. Hamilton added a warning to the technical documentation and proposed a software fix to prevent the error during a real mission. Her proposal was overruled on the grounds that trained astronauts would never make that mistake. During the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during flight, wiping out the onboard navigational data. Hamilton's team was called in to solve the error, and her proposed changes were then integrated into the program. This became an early example of "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton's most famous contribution came during the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised a 1202 alarm: the system was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch. Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software that could shut down unnecessary background tasks to prioritize mission-critical functions. Houston trusted the software and allowed the mission to proceed. Two men walked on the moon for the first time. Hamilton continued at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the lab spun out of MIT to become Draper Laboratory. "Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful," said Jerry M. Wohletz, president and CEO at Draper. "Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home." In 1976, Hamilton founded Higher Order Software, based on her approach of error prevention and fault tolerance. A decade later, she founded Hamilton Technologies, whose flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language for engineering complex software systems. Throughout her career, Hamilton fought for recognition of software engineering as a legitimate discipline. "When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing," she told El Pais in 2018. "It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline." In 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure as part of the Women of NASA set, originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock. "Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. "She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from." She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity. “I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency. Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, first at the Instrumentation Lab and later at Lincoln Laboratory. She authored more than 130 publications and helped establish software engineering as a dedicated field. In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history," the White House citation read. "Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics at the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a bachelor's degree in 1958. She moved to Boston in 1959 and found a temporary position in MIT's meteorology department, working with professor Edward N. Lorenz on weather prediction software. That work later informed Lorenz's pioneering research on chaos theory. In 1961, Hamilton joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory as a programmer on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system. She wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer, which the U.S. Air Force used to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this period, she became interested in software reliability, a concept that was largely unexplored at the time. In 1965, Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw a newspaper advertisement: MIT's Instrumentation Lab was seeking programmers to develop software to send a man to the moon. NASA had awarded the lab the contract to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Hamilton applied and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, and the first female programmer on the project. She initially worked on software for uncrewed Apollo missions, then moved up to lead the team developing onboard flight software for crewed missions. By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, overseeing more than 400 people. "There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. "Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers." Hamilton's approach to software development proved critical during the Apollo missions. One incident, known as "the Lauren error," occurred when her four-year-old daughter Lauren accidentally activated a pre-launch program called P01 while playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab, crashing the simulator midflight. Hamilton added a warning to the technical documentation and proposed a software fix to prevent the error during a real mission. Her proposal was overruled on the grounds that trained astronauts would never make that mistake. Hamilton's team was called in to solve the error, and her proposed changes were then integrated into the program. This became an early example of "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton's most famous contribution came during the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised a 1202 alarm: the system was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch. Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software that could shut down unnecessary background tasks to prioritize mission-critical functions. Wohletz, president and CEO at Draper. "Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home." A decade later, she founded Hamilton Technologies, whose flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language for engineering complex software systems. "When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing," she told El Pais in 2018. "It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas.
