Hamilton joined MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory after earlier programming work in meteorology and at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, where she worked on the SAGE air defense project.

Her interest in software reliability grew during that period, according to MIT News.In 1965, Hamilton joined the Apollo effort after the Instrumentation Laboratory had won a NASA contract to develop onboard flight software.

She became the first programmer hired for the Apollo project and later led teams responsible for software on crewed missions.By 1968, Hamilton was assistant director overseeing the Command and Service Module team, while more than 400 people worked on Apollo software, according to MIT News.
CNN reported that she ultimately led a team of about 100 engineers designing software to guide NASA's Apollo missions.
Hamilton described the software work as an unusually demanding experience because the missions allowed no second chance.

She said the team developed new solutions while working with technology that was still poorly understood."From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009.
Her work included developing approaches to software reliability and defensive programming, according to MIT News.

The Apollo software's architecture became a defining part of Hamilton's contribution to the program.MIT aerospace professor and interim department head Olivier de Weck described Hamilton as a major contributor to Apollo's success and to the development of software engineering.
"To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement.

She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics.Hamilton's influence extended beyond Apollo.

MIT said she authored more than 130 publications and continued working in systems software after leaving the university.Her achievements received national recognition in 2016, when President Barack Obama presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

The White House citation credited her with advancing software engineering and helping make the Apollo lunar missions possible."Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history.
Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon," the Presidential Medal of Freedom citation said.

Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936 and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics with a minor in philosophy from Earlham College in 1958.She moved to Boston in 1959 and began her computing career at MIT.

Lorenz.She later joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961 before moving to the Instrumentation Laboratory and the Apollo program.The NASA contract had sought programmers to develop software to "send man to the moon," according to MIT News.
Hamilton applied for the work and became the first programmer on the Apollo project.Hamilton received numerous honors during her career, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Eliminations for the 15th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals begin at 10 a.m. CT Sunday at World Wide Technology Raceway, and with the NHRA Countdown to the Championship reaching its midpoint, the margin between being prepared and being ready to win has never been smaller. Sunday is the portal through which every championship contender must pass. It is where qualifying promise becomes race-day performance, where momentum takes shape and where teams that are prepared just enough can be outpaced by those that are fully ready to win. The 17th of 20 events in the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series season is also the third of six races in the Countdown to the Championship. By Sunday evening, the title picture in Top Fuel, Funny Car, Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle could look dramatically different. Points leader Shawn Langdon enters eliminations as the No. 1 qualifier in Top Fuel after a 3.679-second run at 339.87 mph. Langdon has won three consecutive races, including the first two events of the Countdown, and will open against eight-time world champion Tony Schumacher. Schumacher qualified 16th with a 3.842, making the opening pairing a meeting between one of the hottest drivers in the sport and the most successful Top Fuel driver in NHRA history. Langdon’s Kalitta Motorsports teammate and closest championship rival, Doug Kalitta, starts from the No. 10 position and draws No. 7 qualifier Shawn Reed, giving the championship rivals very different routes through the ladder. The depth of the Top Fuel field is evident throughout the opening round. No. 2 qualifier Antron Brown faces Clay Millican, while rookie Maddi Gordon, who qualified third with a 3.708 at 340.65 mph, races Will Smith. Tony Stewart meets Josh Hart in a six-versus-11 matchup, and Leah Pruett faces Kyle Wurtzel in the closest pairing of the round, separated by just .001-second in qualifying. Justin Ashley, one of the category’s strongest leavers, qualified 12th and faces No. 5 qualifier Billy Torrence, while Michigan runner-up Spencer Massey opens against Jasmine Salinas. Funny Car may offer the most consequential first-round matchup of the morning. Back-to-back world champion Austin Prock qualified fourth with a 3.882 and will face No. 13 qualifier Ron Capps. Prock is trying to regain ground in the championship, while Capps entered the weekend among the closest challengers to points leader Matt Hagan. One of those title contenders will be finished before the second round. Jack Beckman leads the field with a 3.866 at 332.59 mph and begins eliminations against Dale Creasy Jr. Alexis DeJoria, whose 3.882 at 334.65 mph held the top spot after Friday, qualified second and will race Bobby Bode. Hagan begins Sunday from the No. 3 position against Terry Haddock. The four-time world champion arrives with an 84-point lead after winning at Rockingham and has reached the final round at four consecutive events. Hagan is also the defending St. Louis winner, but Sunday’s ladder offers no guarantees in a category where the top eight qualifiers are separated by only .055-second. Jordan Vandergriff, second in the standings after winning the Countdown opener in Michigan, qualified seventh and faces Cruz Pedregon. J.R. Todd will race Blake Alexander, Chad Green draws Spencer Hyde and Daniel Wilkerson faces Dave Richards in a matchup separated by just .002-second. Pro Stock’s championship fight is even tighter, and the qualifying sheet reflects it. The quickest eight cars are separated by only .016-second, creating an opening round in which reaction times and execution could carry as much weight as qualifying position. Troy Coughlin Jr. earned the No. 1 position with a 6.473 at 211.69 mph and will face Chris Vang. Coughlin opened the Countdown with a victory in Michigan and now has another opportunity to move deeper into the championship conversation. Points leader Greg Stanfield qualified second, just .001-second behind Coughlin, and races Mason McGaha. Defending event winner Greg Anderson starts third against Kenny Delco, while Aaron Stanfield faces Deric Kramer. Two pairings near the center of the ladder could create significant title movement. No. 6 qualifier Eric Latino faces reigning world champion Dallas Glenn, who starts 11th, and No. 8 qualifier Cody Anderson races six-time world champion Erica Enders. Enders owns six St. Louis victories and qualified only .002-second behind Anderson. Matt Hartford, who entered the weekend second in points, opens against Stephen Bell, while Jeg Coughlin Jr. races Matt Latino. In Pro Stock Motorcycle , Gaige Herrera made the category’s loudest qualifying statement with a track-record 6.644 at 202.76 mph. The three-time defending St. Louis winner begins eliminations against Malcolm Phillips Jr. as he tries to erase the 64-point deficit separating him from championship leader and Vance & Hines teammate Richard Gadson. Gadson qualified seventh and immediately faces No. 8 qualifier Chase Van Sant. Only .013-second separated them in qualifying, giving the points leader a demanding opening assignment at a point in the season when every round carries growing championship weight. Matt Smith qualified second with a 6.663 at a track-record speed of 203.12 mph and races Geno Scali. Angie Smith starts fourth against Michigan finalist Marc Ingwersen, while Michigan winner John Hall faces Steve Johnson. Joey Gladstone, Ryan Oehler and Clayton Howey are also positioned to influence a tightly packed championship field. Beyond the Mission Foods Series, Sunday’s program also includes eliminations in the NHRA Lucas Oil Drag Racing Series, the JBS Equipment NHRA Pro Mod Drag Racing Series presented by Elite Motorsports and the Flexjet NHRA Factory Stock Showdown. Fans can take part in the SealMaster Track Walk and the special pre-race ceremonies introducing the drivers competing for a prestigious 75th-anniversary Diamond Wally. Following the final rounds, fans are invited to the winner’s circle celebration to congratulate the newest St. Louis champions. The day will also place NHRA in one of its biggest television windows of the season. Most FOX markets will air the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals from 4:30-6:30 p.m. ET following football, while select markets will receive the race from 2-4 p.m. ET leading directly into football coverage. Qualifying determined where each team will begin. Sunday will reveal which teams are truly ready to step through the portal and perform like champions. Pre-race ceremonies at 9 a.m. NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series eliminations begin at 10 a.m. Sunday, Oct. 4, FOX will televise two hours of final eliminations coverage at either 2 p.m. or 4:30 p.m. ET, depending on the market. 2025 EVENT WINNERS Doug Kalitta, Top Fuel; Matt Hagan, Funny Car; Greg Anderson, Pro Stock; and Gaige Herrera, Pro Stock Motorcycle.

Race Photos from Sunday Eliminations – Final and Winner Circle Race Photos from Sunday Eliminations – Round 1 Shawn Langdon remains the hottest driver in NHRA competition, earning his fourth consecutive victory and eighth win of the 2026 season. The triumph also gives him wins in the opening three events of the six-race Countdown to the Championship playoffs. The No. 1 qualifier powered his dragster to a winning run of 3.732 seconds at 335.90 mph in the final round, defeating Will Smith, whose run was hampered by tire smoke early in the pass. The victory keeps Langdon undefeated at the midway point of the Countdown. “We’ve been good when we needed to be good, but we’ve been great when we needed to be great,” said Langdon. “Every time I hit the gas, I know I’m going to have a really dang good race car. Hopefully I don’t mess that up.” Langdon’s path to victory included wins over Tony Schumacher, Leah Pruett, Justin Ashley, and Smith, securing the 30th victory of his career. “At the beginning of the year, we had some goals in mind for our team, said Langdon. “We’ve been so close the last couple of years [winning a season championship]. We had the equipment, we had the personnel, we had the team to compete for championships, but it just didn’t work in our favor.” His four-race winning streak has expanded his lead in the standings to 116 points over second-place Doug Kalitta, with only three races remaining in the season. The weekend was even more impressive considering that Langdon set a new World Wide Technology Raceway speed record of 341.68 mph during the opening round of eliminations, eclipsing the mark established by Maddi Gordon just one day earlier. “I feel like I’m living a dream right now, but it’s a reality and it’s great to be a part of it,” said Langdon. Austin Prock made a powerful statement in Funny Car competition, reminding the field that he intends to defend his championship. To earn the victory, Prock navigated a challenging lineup that included Ron Capps, J.R. Todd, and No. 1 qualifier Jack Beckman before posting a winning run of 3.909 seconds at 332.84 mph to defeat Jordan Vandergriff in the final round. “We had to run through a lot of hitters today,” said Prock. “Each round was like a final round. Everybody we beat was in front of us in the Countdown. It was an epic way to cap it off. You don’t have days like this very often. When you run through four hitters like that, that’s like winning two races in one.” The victory moved Prock into third place in the Countdown standings, 106 points behind leader Matt Hagan with three races left on the schedule. “This was a big win. For the points, for our family, for our team — this is the time to get hot,” Prock said. “After everything we’ve been through this year, all the hours we haven’t slept and seven days a week working at this, it really pays off when you get a win.” The Pro Stock final featured a memorable father-versus-son showdown between Greg Stanfield and Aaron Stanfield. The elder Stanfield entered the matchup with a commanding 6-1 advantage in head-to-head competition and had previously won their only final-round meeting. However, Aaron turned the tables in St. Louis, winning on a holeshot thanks to a stellar .018-second reaction time. His 6.556-second pass at 209.20 mph narrowly defeated Greg’s .028 reaction time and quicker 6.547-second run at 209.85 mph. “It’s hard to get to the final round alone, and to be able to share it with my dad is pretty special. He’s taught me absolutely everything I know in a race car. I told him I was fixing to show him what he taught me,” Aaron said. “There were a lot of questions about whether we were going to race fair, and questions about if I laid down in the first round last weekend when he won. I think there are a lot of people who need to tip their hat right there. That final round shows what my dad and I are all about. We’re going to race as hard as we can possibly race. A thousandth at the stripe — it doesn’t get any better than that.” Aaron reached the final by defeating Deric Kramer, Matt Hartford, and Troy Coughlin Jr. The win was the 17th of his career and moved him into seventh place in the Countdown standings. “I don’t know what kind of shot I have at winning a championship, but I sure would like to see my dad win won.” said Aaron Stanfield. “He’s fought his whole career for this opportunity. I had to beg him to get back in a Pro Stock car, and obviously he’s still got a lot left in the tank.” Despite the runner-up finish, Greg Stanfield increased his Countdown lead to 71 points over Dallas Green. Gaige Herrera continued his remarkable success at World Wide Technology Raceway, capturing his fourth consecutive victory at the facility. Riding for the Vance & Hines Suzuki team, Herrera faced teammate and Countdown leader Richard Gadson in the final round. “Racing Richard in the final puts a lot of pressure on me,” said Herrera. “He’s the man on the tree. He’s very consistent, and it was awesome to race him in the final.” The victory moved Herrera within 32 points of Gadson in the battle for the season championship. “I felt like I was trying to push myself too much the last couple races,” said Herrera. “This whole weekend, I just reminded myself: I’m living the dream, I’m having fun and that’s what it’s all about.”

Eliminations for the 15th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals begin at 10 a.m. CT Sunday at World Wide Technology Raceway, and with the NHRA Countdown to the Championship reaching its midpoint, the margin between being prepared and being ready to win has never been smaller. Sunday is the portal through which every championship contender must pass. It is where qualifying promise becomes race-day performance, where momentum takes shape and where teams that are prepared just enough can be outpaced by those that are fully ready to win. The 17th of 20 events in the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series season is also the third of six races in the Countdown to the Championship. By Sunday evening, the title picture in Top Fuel, Funny Car, Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle could look dramatically different. Points leader Shawn Langdon enters eliminations as the No. 1 qualifier in Top Fuel after a 3.679-second run at 339.87 mph. Langdon has won three consecutive races, including the first two events of the Countdown, and will open against eight-time world champion Tony Schumacher. Schumacher qualified 16th with a 3.842, making the opening pairing a meeting between one of the hottest drivers in the sport and the most successful Top Fuel driver in NHRA history. Langdon’s Kalitta Motorsports teammate and closest championship rival, Doug Kalitta, starts from the No. 10 position and draws No. 7 qualifier Shawn Reed, giving the championship rivals very different routes through the ladder. The depth of the Top Fuel field is evident throughout the opening round. No. 2 qualifier Antron Brown faces Clay Millican, while rookie Maddi Gordon, who qualified third with a 3.708 at 340.65 mph, races Will Smith. Tony Stewart meets Josh Hart in a six-versus-11 matchup, and Leah Pruett faces Kyle Wurtzel in the closest pairing of the round, separated by just .001-second in qualifying. Justin Ashley, one of the category’s strongest leavers, qualified 12th and faces No. 5 qualifier Billy Torrence, while Michigan runner-up Spencer Massey opens against Jasmine Salinas. Funny Car may offer the most consequential first-round matchup of the morning. Back-to-back world champion Austin Prock qualified fourth with a 3.882 and will face No. 13 qualifier Ron Capps. Prock is trying to regain ground in the championship, while Capps entered the weekend among the closest challengers to points leader Matt Hagan. One of those title contenders will be finished before the second round. Jack Beckman leads the field with a 3.866 at 332.59 mph and begins eliminations against Dale Creasy Jr. Alexis DeJoria, whose 3.882 at 334.65 mph held the top spot after Friday, qualified second and will race Bobby Bode. Hagan begins Sunday from the No. 3 position against Terry Haddock. The four-time world champion arrives with an 84-point lead after winning at Rockingham and has reached the final round at four consecutive events. Hagan is also the defending St. Louis winner, but Sunday’s ladder offers no guarantees in a category where the top eight qualifiers are separated by only .055-second. Jordan Vandergriff, second in the standings after winning the Countdown opener in Michigan, qualified seventh and faces Cruz Pedregon. J.R. Todd will race Blake Alexander, Chad Green draws Spencer Hyde and Daniel Wilkerson faces Dave Richards in a matchup separated by just .002-second. Pro Stock’s championship fight is even tighter, and the qualifying sheet reflects it. The quickest eight cars are separated by only .016-second, creating an opening round in which reaction times and execution could carry as much weight as qualifying position. Troy Coughlin Jr. earned the No. 1 position with a 6.473 at 211.69 mph and will face Chris Vang. Coughlin opened the Countdown with a victory in Michigan and now has another opportunity to move deeper into the championship conversation. Points leader Greg Stanfield qualified second, just .001-second behind Coughlin, and races Mason McGaha. Defending event winner Greg Anderson starts third against Kenny Delco, while Aaron Stanfield faces Deric Kramer. Two pairings near the center of the ladder could create significant title movement. We keep our heads down and keep working hard for the next one. It also includes eliminations coverage on FOX on Sunday. The majority of markets on Sunday, Oct. 4, will see NHRA action from St. Louis following football broadcasts early in the day. Those markets will air the NHRA playoff race from 4:30-6:30 p.m. ET following the football on FOX game, while some markets will air NHRA coverage from 2-4 p.m. ET, leading directly into football on FOX action. Langdon and teammate Kalitta have – for the time being – made it a two-horse race in Top Fuel. Langdon leads Kalitta by just 25 points, but third-place Tony Stewart is a whopping 155 points back of Langdon, showcasing just how dominant Langdon has been for the bulk of the year. The class remains filled with talent, including Antron Brown, Leah Pruett, rookie standout Maddi Gordon, Justin Ashley and Josh Hart, but Langdon and his group have been on a remarkable pace in 2026. Langdon has been driven by coming up just short in the championship chase in recent seasons, looking to stay just a step ahead of Kalitta as the reigning world champion is after a third world title in the past four seasons. “I think we all feed off one another and it’s just a good working environment. We all work well together,” Langdon said. “We had a couple years of finishing second, finishing second in the regular season, and it’s not a bad spot to be, but it definitely gives you something to strive for. Fans can enjoy the special pre-race ceremonies that introduce and celebrate each driver racing for the prestigious Wally on Sunday and includes the fan favorite SealMaster Track Walk, as well as the winner’s circle celebration on Sunday after racing concludes, where fans are invited to congratulate the St. Louis event winners. As always, fans get a pit pass to the most powerful and sensory-filled motorsports attraction. Fans can see their favorite teams in action and servicing their cars between rounds, get autographs from their favorite drivers and more. They can also visit NHRA’s Manufacturers Midway, which includes interactive displays, merchandise, food and fun. NHRA Mission Food Drag Racing Series qualifying will feature two rounds at 4:30 and 7 p.m. CT on Friday, Oct. 2, and the final two rounds on Saturday, Oct. 3 at 12 and 2:30 p.m. Final eliminations are scheduled for 10 a.m. CT on Sunday, Oct. 4. Tickets may be purchased at the WWTR ticket office, by phone at (618) 215-8888, or online at www.wwtraceway.com . All children 12 and under are free in the general admission area with a paid adult. NHRA provides competition opportunities for drivers of all levels in the NHRA Summit Racing Series and NHRA Street Legal™. NHRA also offers the NHRA Jr. Street® program for teens and the Summit Racing Jr. Drag Racing League® for youth ages 5 to 17. With more than 100 Member Tracks, NHRA allows racers to compete at a variety of locations nationally and internationally. NHRA’s Youth and Education Services® (YES) Program reaches over 30,000 students annually to ignite their interest in automotive and racing related careers. NHRA’s streaming service, NHRA.tv ®, allows fans to view all NHRA national events as well as exclusive features of the sport. In addition, NHRA owns and operates three racing facilities: Gainesville Raceway in Florida; Lucas Oil Indianapolis Raceway Park; and In-N-Out Burger Pomona Dragstrip in Southern California. Race Photos from Sunday Eliminations – Final and Winner Circle Race Photos from Sunday Eliminations – Round 1 Shawn Langdon remains the hottest driver in NHRA competition, earning his fourth consecutive victory and eighth win of the 2026 season. The triumph also gives him wins in the opening three events of the six-race Countdown to the Championship playoffs. The No. 1 qualifier powered his dragster to a winning run of 3.732 seconds at 335.90 mph in the final round, defeating Will Smith, whose run was hampered by tire smoke early in the pass. The victory keeps Langdon undefeated at the midway point of the Countdown. “We’ve been good when we needed to be good, but we’ve been great when we needed to be great,” said Langdon. “Every time I hit the gas, I know I’m going to have a really dang good race car. Hopefully I don’t mess that up.” Langdon’s path to victory included wins over Tony Schumacher, Leah Pruett, Justin Ashley, and Smith, securing the 30th victory of his career. “At the beginning of the year, we had some goals in mind for our team, said Langdon. “We’ve been so close the last couple of years [winning a season championship]. We had the equipment, we had the personnel, we had the team to compete for championships, but it just didn’t work in our favor.” His four-race winning streak has expanded his lead in the standings to 116 points over second-place Doug Kalitta, with only three races remaining in the season. The weekend was even more impressive considering that Langdon set a new World Wide Technology Raceway speed record of 341.68 mph during the opening round of eliminations, eclipsing the mark established by Maddi Gordon just one day earlier. “I feel like I’m living a dream right now, but it’s a reality and it’s great to be a part of it,” said Langdon. Austin Prock made a powerful statement in Funny Car competition, reminding the field that he intends to defend his championship. To earn the victory, Prock navigated a challenging lineup that included Ron Capps, J.R. Todd, and No. 1 qualifier Jack Beckman before posting a winning run of 3.909 seconds at 332.84 mph to defeat Jordan Vandergriff in the final round. “We had to run through a lot of hitters today,” said Prock. “Each round was like a final round. Everybody we beat was in front of us in the Countdown. It was an epic way to cap it off. You don’t have days like this very often. When you run through four hitters like that, that’s like winning two races in one.” The victory moved Prock into third place in the Countdown standings, 106 points behind leader Matt Hagan with three races left on the schedule. “This was a big win. For the points, for our family, for our team — this is the time to get hot,” Prock said. “After everything we’ve been through this year, all the hours we haven’t slept and seven days a week working at this, it really pays off when you get a win.” The Pro Stock final featured a memorable father-versus-son showdown between Greg Stanfield and Aaron Stanfield. The elder Stanfield entered the matchup with a commanding 6-1 advantage in head-to-head competition and had previously won their only final-round meeting. However, Aaron turned the tables in St. Louis, winning on a holeshot thanks to a stellar .018-second reaction time. His 6.556-second pass at 209.20 mph narrowly defeated Greg’s .028 reaction time and quicker 6.547-second run at 209.85 mph. “It’s hard to get to the final round alone, and to be able to share it with my dad is pretty special. He’s taught me absolutely everything I know in a race car. I told him I was fixing to show him what he taught me,” Aaron said. “There were a lot of questions about whether we were going to race fair, and questions about if I laid down in the first round last weekend when he won. I think there are a lot of people who need to tip their hat right there. That final round shows what my dad and I are all about. We’re going to race as hard as we can possibly race. A thousandth at the stripe — it doesn’t get any better than that.” Aaron reached the final by defeating Deric Kramer, Matt Hartford, and Troy Coughlin Jr. The win was the 17th of his career and moved him into seventh place in the Countdown standings. “I don’t know what kind of shot I have at winning a championship, but I sure would like to see my dad win won.” said Aaron Stanfield. “He’s fought his whole career for this opportunity. I had to beg him to get back in a Pro Stock car, and obviously he’s still got a lot left in the tank.” Despite the runner-up finish, Greg Stanfield increased his Countdown lead to 71 points over Dallas Green. Gaige Herrera continued his remarkable success at World Wide Technology Raceway, capturing his fourth consecutive victory at the facility. Riding for the Vance & Hines Suzuki team, Herrera faced teammate and Countdown leader Richard Gadson in the final round. “Racing Richard in the final puts a lot of pressure on me,” said Herrera. “He’s the man on the tree. He’s very consistent, and it was awesome to race him in the final.” The victory moved Herrera within 32 points of Gadson in the battle for the season championship. “I felt like I was trying to push myself too much the last couple races,” said Herrera. “This whole weekend, I just reminded myself: I’m living the dream, I’m having fun and that’s what it’s all about.”

For 2026, Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (GOOGL) now projects that it will lay out between $175 billion and $185 billion on capital expenditures -- nearly double the amount it spent on them in 2025. That massive budget, which will largely go toward data centers, networking equipment, AI processors, and servers, is meant to keep the tech giant at the front of the pack in the increasingly expensive artificial intelligence (AI) race. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » But is this extensive infrastructure buildout a strategic masterstroke or a big mistake? The tech world is full of examples of companies that don't adapt to innovation quickly enough. Kodak had the chance to get into digital cameras early, but failed to. BlackBerry dismissed touchscreens. Blockbuster didn't take video streaming seriously. Executives are well aware of those history lessons and want to avoid having their businesses become case studies of what happens when a company doesn't adjust in time. If the value that AI winds up delivering lives up to the hype, Alphabet will have a solid foothold in that market that it will be able to enhance as it makes more investments. It has the chips and cloud services other companies need for the AI buildout, with its cloud division in particular offering a bright spot. In Q4 2025, Google Cloud revenue increased 48% year over year to $17.6 billion, and the segment's operating income increased 30.1% to $5.3 billion. Another proof point for Alphabet's cloud strength for AI use can be found in its backlog. "Google Cloud's backlog increased 55% sequentially and more than doubled year over year, reaching $240 billion at the end of the fourth quarter," said CFO Anat Ashkenazi on the company's Q4 earnings call. "The increase in backlog was driven by strong demand for our cloud products, led by our enterprise AI offerings, from multiple customers." It also has its own in-house products that it can optimize and monetize using AI, such as Google Search . Whenever you invest in a company, it's exciting to think about what can go right, but what's equally important, if not more so, is considering what can go wrong. There are several risks that come with Alphabet's impressive spending plans. One is that Wall Street may not have the patience to let the narrative fully play out before reaching a verdict on the stock. For example, Alphabet delivered what was generally considered a strong Q4 report, beating consensus top and bottom-line expectations. The stock price still took a hit, however, as management announced the scale of its 2026 capital expenditure plans. On Feb. 4, the day of the earnings announcement, Alphabet's Class A shares opened at $342.96. The next day, they opened 9% lower at at $312.09. That shows how much short-term concern can weigh down the stock price, but the biggest risk for the tech giant is that demand for AI processing power might not live up to expectations in the long term. If AI demand isn't at the levels expected for all the big tech players building out the infrastructure, the fears that they have been overspending could prove prophetic. As one of the companies with one of the biggest spending plans, Alphabet could be hit especially hard. Since the AI race started, Alphabet has been in a precarious position. One of the narratives early in the AI race was that Alphabet was caught flat-footed by OpenAI's launch of ChatGPT. Alphabet shifted that perception last year, and its shares rebounded, climbing roughly 66%. For 2026, one predominant theme in the market is worry that tech giants are spending too much on AI infrastructure when they may not reap strong enough returns on those investments. To separate the noise from what matters in this case, it helps to consider Alphabet's financial situation. It isn't a risky start-up going all-in on a speculative technology that will either make it or break it. It's generating huge profits in the here and now, with net income of $132 billion in 2025, a 32% increase from 2024. It also has diverse revenue sources and a bankroll that should allow it to navigate any setbacks and stumbles it encounters. Overall, whether you believe Alphabet needs to ramp up its spending or cut back on it, this will still require more than a quarter-to-quarter mindset as we all watch to see how it plays out. That massive budget, which will largely go toward data centers, networking equipment, AI processors, and servers, is meant to keep the tech giant at the front of the pack in the increasingly expensive artificial intelligence (AI) race. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » But is this extensive infrastructure buildout a strategic masterstroke or a big mistake? The tech world is full of examples of companies that don't adapt to innovation quickly enough. Kodak had the chance to get into digital cameras early, but failed to. BlackBerry dismissed touchscreens. Blockbuster didn't take video streaming seriously. Executives are well aware of those history lessons and want to avoid having their businesses become case studies of what happens when a company doesn't adjust in time. If the value that AI winds up delivering lives up to the hype, Alphabet will have a solid foothold in that market that it will be able to enhance as it makes more investments. It has the chips and cloud services other companies need for the AI buildout, with its cloud division in particular offering a bright spot. In Q4 2025, Google Cloud revenue increased 48% year over year to $17.6 billion, and the segment's operating income increased 30.1% to $5.3 billion. Another proof point for Alphabet's cloud strength for AI use can be found in its backlog. "Google Cloud's backlog increased 55% sequentially and more than doubled year over year, reaching $240 billion at the end of the fourth quarter," said CFO Anat Ashkenazi on the company's Q4 earnings call. "The increase in backlog was driven by strong demand for our cloud products, led by our enterprise AI offerings, from multiple customers." It also has its own in-house products that it can optimize and monetize using AI, such as Google Search . Whenever you invest in a company, it's exciting to think about what can go right, but what's equally important, if not more so, is considering what can go wrong. There are several risks that come with Alphabet's impressive spending plans. One is that Wall Street may not have the patience to let the narrative fully play out before reaching a verdict on the stock. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC.

When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum.

Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it.

Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically.

Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk.
A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder.

But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs.

Those $25 billion in crypto assets spread across Robinhood's customer custody wallets belong entirely to Robinhood's customers — Robinhood holds the private keys, but the coins are not on Robinhood's own books.The $25 million corporate BTC purchase is a different category.

The distinction matters for both accounting and risk: customer custody creates zero direct P&L exposure for Robinhood (it earns custody-related revenue from fees and services, not from BTC price movements).

He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range. So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate. Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026. A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap. The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform. That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it. The accounting environment is part of the reason. Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose. A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold. That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under ASU 2023-08, in-scope crypto assets — Bitcoin included — must be measured at fair value at every reporting date, with gains and losses flowing through net income each quarter. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC. Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices. In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined. When BTC drops, Robinhood's trading volumes compress and its crypto transaction revenue contracts. This has been true since the company launched crypto trading.What is new is that the $25 million corporate Bitcoin position is now marked to market every quarter under ASU 2023-08. Nasdaq-listed Strategy MSTR $154.55 · Market Closed started this trend in 2020 and now its followed by more than 170 firms worldwide.

extraction.body: Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it. He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range. So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate. Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026. A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap. The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform. That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it. The accounting environment is part of the reason. Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose. A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold. That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024. “Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion [range].
The move puts Robinhood among a growing cohort of public companies holding BTC as a treasury asset.
Nasdaq-listed Strategy MSTR $154.55 · Market Closed started this trend in 2020 and now its followed by more than 170 firms worldwide.

sources.title: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 Instrument: Hands-on, Videos, Why it’s Different - CDM Create Digital Music
passages: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware.
It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths .
It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique.

It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.
The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly.
Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise.
I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now.
The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.
The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage.
A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport.
But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away.
Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback .
And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced .
Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware.
Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special.
Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM :
The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way.
Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible.
Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing.
There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating.
I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real.
Some of the little touches I was able to glean:
Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results.

extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special. Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

coreStoryFacts.text: Teenage Engineering founder and CEO Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety that it plans to stop making synths.

Launched in 2011, it put Teenage Engineering on the map and has been central to its success ever since. > “Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’ But I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business,” Kouthoofd says.
“We can be so much more than that.” Teenage Engineering did not immediately return a request for comment.
Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware.
It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths .
It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique.

It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.
The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly.
Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise.
I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now.
The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.
The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage.
A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport.
But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away.
Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback .
And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced .
Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware.
Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special.
Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM :
The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way.
Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing.
There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating.
I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real.

extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special. Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.

The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product.
Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo .

In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean:

You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix.

It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special.

Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.)

And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.)
Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM :

The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.

It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come):

The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate.

All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying:
The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information…
Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza

And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core?
Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change.
CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

sources.title: Why Packaging Is Now a Frontline Issue in Pharma Supply Chains
passages: This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed.
Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle.
Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit.
There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging.
These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm.
The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control.

extraction.body: Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle. At the same time, the logistics environments they move through are becoming less stable. On the surface, many of these challenges appear to be logistics problems. Protecting high-value medications, biologics and personalized medicines goes beyond packaging alone. The cold chain is no longer a controlled environment; it is a dynamic system operating under constant disruption. Packaging Is No Longer a Passive Layer — It Requires Oversight In the 100 years since the dawn of electric refrigeration, humans' ability to keep things cool has advanced significantly. There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging. The problem is that these systems were built on assumptions. Their success assumes that a shipment will move within a defined transit window, that exposure conditions will stay within tested ranges, or that handoffs between partners will happen as planned. These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm. Here’s what those breakdowns can look like in practice: A biologic shipment delayed at an airport transfer hub can sit on a tarmac for hours in high heat. A shipment flagged for inspection may experience temperature fluctuations that packaging was never designed to absorb. In each case, the shipment's packaging still does exactly what it was designed to do. But ultimately, packaging can only perform within its limits, and those limits are often pushed to the edge of what they can withstand. This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed. How Are Advanced Therapies Exposing Blind Spots in Cold Chain Control? The shift in cold chain risk starts with the shipments themselves. Biologics, cell and gene therapies and personalized medicine have redefined acceptable risk in pharmaceutical logistics. Many require strict temperature control at minus 20 C, minus 80 C or below. For logistics providers handling advanced therapies at scale, this risk profile leaves no margin for error. One operator managing tens of thousands of life sciences shipments annually ultimately moved to real-time monitoring across all shipments because, in their mind, there is simply no option for failure when transporting cell and gene therapies. The difference between product loss and recovery is timing. Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit. Packaging is designed to protect within expected conditions; it cannot adapt to compounded delays, exposure or handling variability. This assumes that what happens during shipping (and between actual checkpoints) is stable — and if it’s not, there’s no way to adapt. Continuous monitoring of temperature, location and environmental conditions enables teams to see where risk is developing, not just that it occurred. For example, when a shipment is delayed at a transfer hub, real-time data can show both the current temperature and the rate of change. Teams can estimate how much thermal protection remains and determine whether intervention is required. With visibility, teams can act while a shipment is still recoverable. One company noted that before implementing real-time tracking, “we had no real way to understand what happened” when shipments were delayed. With full visibility, teams can now trace exactly where and how disruptions occur — and intervene accordingly. When analyzed over time, shipment data reveal patterns. Addressing them often reduces risk more effectively than changing packaging alone. Why Does Control Now Depend on Visibility, Response and System Design? The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control. For years, protection was measured by whether packaging could hold temperature under expected conditions.

sources.title: Ethereum news: Tom Lee says Bitmine to soon stop buying ETH - CoinDesk
passages: Bitmine chairman Tom Lee, speaking Wednesday at TOKEN2049 in Singapore, said the firm will stop accumulating ETH once its holdings reach 5% of the token’s circulating supply, setting a hard ceiling on a buying spree that has made the company one of the world’s largest ETH holders.
The looming end of Bitmine’s purchases matters because the company has provided unusually steady demand.
Bitmine says it has bought ETH every week since launching its ether treasury strategy in June 2025.
At ether’s Wednesday price around $2,580, that stack is worth about $15.5 billion.
However, much of the purchases happened during last year’s crypto bull market at higher prices, meaning Bitmine is sitting deeply underwater on its ether bet.
The firm’s ETH holdings carry $4.5 billion in unrealized losses, according to data collected by DropsTab .
At last week’s buying pace, adding another 100,000 ETH would take about six to seven more weeks, assuming the company continues to accumulate at roughly the same rate.
Ether was already under pressure on Wednesday amid broader crypto market weakness.
ETH fell 5% over the past 24 hours to its weakest price since Sept.
