extraction.body: Get ready for more AI in your Windows and more AI on the desktop. In its first live event in two years, Microsoft today announced its newest Surface laptop, outlined a host of changes coming to Windows 11, and shared a vision of how local-AI and agentic workflows could reshape personal computing for those in the dev community as well as home enthusiasts. Originally teased in May 2026 , the new Surface Laptop Ultra will be Microsoft’s first offering to take advantage of the new Nvidia RTX Spark SoC (system on a chip). The device has a starting price of $2,599, and comes in various SoC and memory configurations, with either a 5120-core or 6144-core Blackwell GPU and up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified memory. It will begin shipping on October 16 and is available for pre-order now. While the new Ultra is clearly focused on the developer crowd, graphical performance was highlighted during the presentation to show off just how capable the laptop can be. By leaning on unified memory allocation rather than the physical VRAM limits of a traditional GPU, the laptop can assign its resources to handle modern gaming tasks as well as local AI development and deployment. The new Gears of War: E-Day was shown running on the system, meaning that even without a traditional gaming GPU, AAA titles are on the table. Joined on stage by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, President of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri also unveiled the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box. This is a $5,999 anodized aluminum black box “designed to meet the needs of frontier developers.” The Spark Dev Box ships with a custom “developer-optimized” build of Windows 11 pre-configured for AI development and local AI use. With 128GB of unified memory and the onboard Nvidia RTX GPU, the box claims one petaflop (that’s 1,000 teraflops) of AI compute performance. The RTX Spark Dev Box’s design is quite sleek. The unit physically resembles something like an Android TV box or game console more than it does a traditional PC. In fact, the vent pattern on the top of the unit is reminiscent of what you see looking down at the top of an Xbox Series X. According to Microsoft’s provided press materials, the venting on the RTX Spark Dev box has 1,000 chassis air vents as a nod to the 1,000 teraflops of AI performance. Outside of the hardware announcements, Microsoft outlined a host of changes headed for Windows 11 this fall. OS builds featured on the Surface Ultra and Spark Box will arrive with an updated Windows software suite to support local model testing out of the box. Microsoft’s baked-in Windows AI, Copilot, is getting a major overhaul. The new Copilot layout will see things divided into three tabs: Coming to a Windows PC later this year, the new update will allow Windows users to execute system-level tasks directly from the search bar. Rather than opening up something like Control Panel to adjust display settings, the user will presumably be able to describe the action they want and have the system execute it directly from the taskbar tray. For those who might still feel a little trepidation about turning over their entire digital lives and files to AI bots, Microsoft announced the availability of Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), a security framework designed to keep agent activities confined to a sandbox. Available to developers today, the framework allows system admins and organizations to monitor active agents working within their systems and to specifically set guardrails for each, ensuring control over exactly what each agent is able to access. MXC acts as a policy layer that directs compute traffic to the appropriate isolation backend. Depending on the workload, MXC can shift to a process container, session container, WSL container, or even an experimental hardware-backed isolation called MicroVM. Bringing all of this new agentic workflow together with traditional Windows is a concept that Microsoft calls “Hybrid Intelligence,” which is a move away from cloud-backed AI solutions and a move toward local ones. Hybrid Intelligence will allow Surface Laptop Ultra or RTX Spark Dev Box users to allocate memory as they see fit for any specific application, as well as offer native support for local frameworks like llama.cpp and models from the Deepseek and Nvidia Nemotron families. Microsoft is betting big on local AI with the changes announced today, but questions about security and user acceptance still remain, especially in light of their past missteps and other recent AI agent mishaps . The Surface Laptop Ultra hits shelves next week—keep an eye out for our review, and we’ll try to figure out whether it’s worth the $2,599 entry price and what this local AI capability buys you. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

extraction.body: Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners. SynthID is a necessary tool as AI content has taken hold of heavy portions of the internet. Models have evolved so much that it’s nearly impossible to tell whether some videos or photos are even real, and it has you second-guessing whether real ones are generated. SynthID takes aim at that problem by introducing invisible watermarks at the generation stage, and when used on an image, it will detect those watermarks. Of course, that only works if the image generation tool inserts its own footprint to begin with. Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future. The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection. According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility. The new SynthID will work with content generated on Google’s own Gemini, a given, as well as content from more partners. So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple. That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together. Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models. But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media.

SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations.

While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google.

Advances in generative AI are making it possible for people to create content in entirely new ways — from text to high quality audio, images and videos. As these capabilities advance and become more broadly available, questions of authenticity, context and verification emerge. Today we’re announcing SynthID Detector, a verification portal to quickly and efficiently identify AI-generated content made with Google AI. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media. It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID. When we launched SynthID — a state-of-the-art tool that embeds imperceptible watermarks and enables the identification of AI-generated content — our aim was to provide a suite of novel technical solutions to help minimise misinformation and misattribution. SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations. While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google. Over 10 billion pieces of content have already been watermarked with SynthID. When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark. If a watermark is detected, the portal will highlight specific portions of the content most likely to be watermarked. For audio, the portal pinpoints specific segments where a SynthID watermark is detected, and for images, it indicates areas where a watermark is most likely. We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly. Journalists, media professionals and researchers can join our waitlist to gain access to the SynthID Detector. To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models. And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com . This means that more content across the web has SynthID embedded in it, not just content generated by Google. At the same time, it’s important that other partners will be able to detect when a piece of content has been watermarked with SynthID. That’s why today we’re also announcing our partnership with GetReal Security , the world’s leading content verification platform. Content transparency remains a complex challenge. To continue to inform and empower people engaging with AI-generated content, we believe it’s vital to continue collaborating with the AI community and broaden access to transparency tools. The author would like to thank Miguel de Andrés-Clavera and the Google Partner Innovation team for their assistance in developing the SynthID Detector portal. Product in development; final product details may differ. Video and text watermark detection will be rolled out in the coming weeks.

sources.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
passages: Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic .
SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.
It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though.
Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.
You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts.
While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it.
Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.”
Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools.
The website will have a disclaimer saying as much.
It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio.
This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually.
Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.
The previous detection tools had a similar limit.
Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools.
The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar.
This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow.
Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that.

VP, Science and Strategic Initiatives, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Advances in generative AI are making it possible for people to create content in entirely new ways — from text to high quality audio, images and videos. As these capabilities advance and become more broadly available, questions of authenticity, context and verification emerge. Today we’re announcing SynthID Detector, a verification portal to quickly and efficiently identify AI-generated content made with Google AI. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media. It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID. When we launched SynthID — a state-of-the-art tool that embeds imperceptible watermarks and enables the identification of AI-generated content — our aim was to provide a suite of novel technical solutions to help minimise misinformation and misattribution. SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations. While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google. Over 10 billion pieces of content have already been watermarked with SynthID. When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark. If a watermark is detected, the portal will highlight specific portions of the content most likely to be watermarked. For audio, the portal pinpoints specific segments where a SynthID watermark is detected, and for images, it indicates areas where a watermark is most likely. We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly. Journalists, media professionals and researchers can join our waitlist to gain access to the SynthID Detector. To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models. And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com . This means that more content across the web has SynthID embedded in it, not just content generated by Google. At the same time, it’s important that other partners will be able to detect when a piece of content has been watermarked with SynthID. That’s why today we’re also announcing our partnership with GetReal Security , the world’s leading content verification platform. Content transparency remains a complex challenge. To continue to inform and empower people engaging with AI-generated content, we believe it’s vital to continue collaborating with the AI community and broaden access to transparency tools. The author would like to thank Miguel de Andrés-Clavera and the Google Partner Innovation team for their assistance in developing the SynthID Detector portal. Product in development; final product details may differ. Video and text watermark detection will be rolled out in the coming weeks.

story.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally

facts.text: Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models.
But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.
Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future.
The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection.
According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.
So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple.

That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.
Stay up to date on news from Google headquarters…
SynthID Detector — a new portal to help identify AI-generated content
The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media.
It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID.
SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations.

While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google.
The author would like to thank Miguel de Andrés-Clavera and the Google Partner Innovation team for their assistance in developing the SynthID Detector portal.
Content transparency remains a complex challenge.
We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly.
When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark.

And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com .
To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models.
The tool checks images, video, and audio files for Google’s SynthID watermark , a system that embeds a near-invisible marker into AI-generated content.
Google first made its SynthID Detector available to media professionals last year, but now anyone can use it by logging into synthid.com .

Microsoft ( MSFT ) unveiled its Nvidia ( NVDA )-powered Surface Laptop Ultra during an event in San Francisco, Calif., on Wednesday. Designed to compete with Apple's ( AAPL ) MacBook Pro laptops for AI, video workloads, and gaming, the $2,599 Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most powerful Surface to date, thanks to its Arm ( ARM )-based Nvidia RTX Spark processor. Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices, Pavan Davuluri, said the chip features up to a staggering 128GB of unified memory, giving it the ability to run demanding AI models that other laptops can't. According to Tom Mainelli, IDC's group vice president of device and consumer research, the Surface Laptop Ultra will likely appeal to early adopters across both the consumer and enterprise spaces. "Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance. "But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers." Orchestration is the process of determining which AI models and agents to use, when, and for what purpose. For instance, you wouldn't want to use an expensive cloud-based model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to perform a task that a free, local model installed on your PC can handle. During Wednesday's event, Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices explained that the company is bringing hybrid AI capabilities and AI agent security to Windows via a series of updates. The enterprise and consumer tech industries have been leaning heavily into local AI models as an alternative to cloud-based models and agents. Kicking off a new arms race in the laptop and desktop space. Microsoft demonstrated the Surface Laptop Ultra's performance in a video clip showing it running the video game "Gears of War: E Day," GitHub Copilot, and the video editing platform DaVinci Resolve at the same time, something that would chew up a standard laptop. When it comes to AI specifically, Microsoft says the Surface Laptop Ultra offers 4.3x faster AI image generation than a MacBook Pro with Apple's M5 Pro chip and 6.2x faster video generation. The PC industry, like the rest of the tech sector, is contending with the ongoing shortage of memory and storage chips. That's forced companies to raise the prices of their devices, cutting into overall sales. But, so far, those increased prices have helped insulate device makers from the worst of the sales declines. sources.title: What To Expect At Microsoft's Windows, Surface And AI Event On October 7 - Engadget
passages: It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least.
This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 .

Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive.
We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here .
We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge.
However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality.
The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs .
NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops.
It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want.
That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw .
I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra.

extraction.body: Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time. On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.) Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7. The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them. Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event. Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.” He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.” The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley. Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800. Microsoft ( MSFT ) unveiled its Nvidia ( NVDA )-powered Surface Laptop Ultra during an event in San Francisco, Calif., on Wednesday. Designed to compete with Apple's ( AAPL ) MacBook Pro laptops for AI, video workloads, and gaming, the $2,599 Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most powerful Surface to date, thanks to its Arm ( ARM )-based Nvidia RTX Spark processor. Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices, Pavan Davuluri, said the chip features up to a staggering 128GB of unified memory, giving it the ability to run demanding AI models that other laptops can't. According to Tom Mainelli, IDC's group vice president of device and consumer research, the Surface Laptop Ultra will likely appeal to early adopters across both the consumer and enterprise spaces. "Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance. "But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers." Orchestration is the process of determining which AI models and agents to use, when, and for what purpose. For instance, you wouldn't want to use an expensive cloud-based model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to perform a task that a free, local model installed on your PC can handle. During Wednesday's event, Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices explained that the company is bringing hybrid AI capabilities and AI agent security to Windows via a series of updates. The enterprise and consumer tech industries have been leaning heavily into local AI models as an alternative to cloud-based models and agents. Kicking off a new arms race in the laptop and desktop space. Microsoft demonstrated the Surface Laptop Ultra's performance in a video clip showing it running the video game "Gears of War: E Day," GitHub Copilot, and the video editing platform DaVinci Resolve at the same time, something that would chew up a standard laptop. When it comes to AI specifically, Microsoft says the Surface Laptop Ultra offers 4.3x faster AI image generation than a MacBook Pro with Apple's M5 Pro chip and 6.2x faster video generation. The PC industry, like the rest of the tech sector, is contending with the ongoing shortage of memory and storage chips. That's forced companies to raise the prices of their devices, cutting into overall sales. But, so far, those increased prices have helped insulate device makers from the worst of the sales declines. It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least. This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 . Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive. Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here . NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops. The Surface Laptop Ultra, which was announced in June , is one of the first devices powered by RTX Spark, and from the brief glimpse we got earlier this year, it appears to be a direct competitor to Apple's powerful MacBook Pro. It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want. But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch). Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. To recap, the NVIDIA RTX Spark will feature 6,144 Blackwell GPU cores, 20 Arm CPU cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power. I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra. Aside from being one of the first systems with RTX Spark, it just seems to be another premium laptop. But I'm hoping to discover what inspired this poetic take on the notebook from Microsoft Corporate Vice President Brett Ostrum: "A machine like this should not sit still. It should be pushed. Taken to the edge. Used to make real what others call impossible. It belongs in the hands of world makers." Microsoft isn't really keeping this a secret: The company wants us to know it's going to have some big agentic AI news next week. That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw . Much like it did with Recall, Microsoft could easily run into unforeseen privacy issues with a true AI agent, which would potentially be able to see all of your files, your browsing history and act on your behalf. We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge. However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality. The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs . The core idea of agentic AI — letting an AI tool work on tasks with minimal input — sounds intriguing, especially to people who've already fully changed their workflows around modern AI models. But it's also not something that will easily translate to people outside of the tech world. I can see why so many programmers got excited about OpenClaw , but only a few people will want to manage an agent with an archaic command line interface.

Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here .

NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops. The Surface Laptop Ultra, which was announced in June , is one of the first devices powered by RTX Spark, and from the brief glimpse we got earlier this year, it appears to be a direct competitor to Apple's powerful MacBook Pro. It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want.

But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch).

Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. To recap, the NVIDIA RTX Spark will feature 6,144 Blackwell GPU cores, 20 Arm CPU cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power.

I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra. Aside from being one of the first systems with RTX Spark, it just seems to be another premium laptop. But I'm hoping to discover what inspired this poetic take on the notebook from Microsoft Corporate Vice President Brett Ostrum: "A machine like this should not sit still. It should be pushed. Taken to the edge. Used to make real what others call impossible. It belongs in the hands of world makers."

Microsoft isn't really keeping this a secret: The company wants us to know it's going to have some big agentic AI news next week. That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw . Much like it did with Recall, Microsoft could easily run into unforeseen privacy issues with a true AI agent, which would potentially be able to see all of your files, your browsing history and act on your behalf.

We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge. However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality. The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs .

The core idea of agentic AI — letting an AI tool work on tasks with minimal input — sounds intriguing, especially to people who've already fully changed their workflows around modern AI models. But it's also not something that will easily translate to people outside of the tech world. I can see why so many programmers got excited about OpenClaw , but only a few people will want to manage an agent with an archaic command line interface.

passages: SpaceX may have a larger opportunity in the long-run.
But for 2027 specifically, Nvidia is my better stock to buy.
The reason isn't that SpaceX lacks meaningful catalysts.
SpaceX is simultaneously scaling Starlink, building AI data centers, developing Starship, expanding government operations, and pursuing space-based infrastructure.
If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.
While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see.
For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup.
SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027.

extraction.body: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now . Microsoft 365 Copilot is becoming a daily habit for people around the world—already, nearly 70% of Fortune 500 companies are using it. Dow anticipates that Copilot will save it millions of dollars on shipping operations in the first year; at Bank of Queensland Group , 70% of users are saving two and a half to five hours per week; Eaton is speeding up internal documentation processes by 83%; and Accenture is going big, rolling out Copilot to 100,000 employees. Today at Microsoft Ignite 2024 , we’re accelerating our ambition to empower every employee with Copilot as a personal assistant and to transform every business process with agents built in Microsoft Copilot Studio. These announcements build on our wave 2 momentum, including the new autonomous agent capabilities that we announced in October 2024 . Thanks to our customers, we have the world’s best feedback loop on AI at work. We’ve dramatically improved Copilot performance—responses are two times faster on average and response satisfaction is nearly three times higher 1 —and shipped hundreds of new features. And we’re adding new value to Copilot to tackle work’s biggest pain points and help every employee scale their impact—from automating repetitive tasks to managing your calendar. Copilot is where you interact with agents , and Copilot Studio is where you can easily create, manage, and connect agents to Copilot. We’re introducing agents in Microsoft 365 designed to help scale individual impact and transform business processes. These new agents complement the autonomous agents that we announced in October 2024 for sales, service, finance, and supply chain professionals—and we’re just getting started. We’ll create many more agents in the coming year that will give customers the competitive advantage they need to future-proof their organization. Chief information officers and IT professionals are at the epicenter of AI transformation. To empower every IT team to lead at scale, we’re introducing the Copilot Control System —designed for IT to confidently adopt and accelerate the business value of Copilot and agents. sources.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
passages: At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text.
It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

Microsoft announced the Surface Laptop Ultra at the event, a machine equipped with Nvidia RTX Spark silicon aimed at improved AI performance.
Microsoft has also emphasized agent workspaces and user-controlled settings, designs intended to keep privacy and security in the foreground.

passages: Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent.
For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways.
Microsoft has unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, a set of software orchestration tools that will let your PC run AI models locally.
Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios.
This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.
It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

sources.title: Microsoft's Hybrid Intelligence gives Copilot more control over your files
passages: Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent.
For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways.
Microsoft has unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, a set of software orchestration tools that will let your PC run AI models locally.
Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios.
This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.
It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech.

Her work helped land humans on the moon and established software engineering as a formal discipline. Margaret Hamilton, the MIT computer scientist who led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept. 30. She was 90. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, first at the Instrumentation Lab and later at Lincoln Laboratory. She authored more than 130 publications and helped establish software engineering as a dedicated field. In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history," the White House citation read. "Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics at the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a bachelor's degree in 1958. She moved to Boston in 1959 and found a temporary position in MIT's meteorology department, working with professor Edward N. Lorenz on weather prediction software. That work later informed Lorenz's pioneering research on chaos theory. In 1961, Hamilton joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory as a programmer on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system. She wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer, which the U.S. Air Force used to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this period, she became interested in software reliability, a concept that was largely unexplored at the time. In 1965, Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw a newspaper advertisement: MIT's Instrumentation Lab was seeking programmers to develop software to send a man to the moon. NASA had awarded the lab the contract to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Hamilton applied and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, and the first female programmer on the project. She initially worked on software for uncrewed Apollo missions, then moved up to lead the team developing onboard flight software for crewed missions. By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, overseeing more than 400 people. "There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. "Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers." Hamilton's approach to software development proved critical during the Apollo missions. One incident, known as "the Lauren error," occurred when her four-year-old daughter Lauren accidentally activated a pre-launch program called P01 while playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab, crashing the simulator midflight. Hamilton added a warning to the technical documentation and proposed a software fix to prevent the error during a real mission. Her proposal was overruled on the grounds that trained astronauts would never make that mistake. During the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during flight, wiping out the onboard navigational data. Hamilton's team was called in to solve the error, and her proposed changes were then integrated into the program. This became an early example of "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton's most famous contribution came during the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised a 1202 alarm: the system was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch. Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software that could shut down unnecessary background tasks to prioritize mission-critical functions. Houston trusted the software and allowed the mission to proceed. Two men walked on the moon for the first time. Hamilton continued at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the lab spun out of MIT to become Draper Laboratory. "Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful," said Jerry M. Wohletz, president and CEO at Draper. "Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home." In 1976, Hamilton founded Higher Order Software, based on her approach of error prevention and fault tolerance. A decade later, she founded Hamilton Technologies, whose flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language for engineering complex software systems. Throughout her career, Hamilton fought for recognition of software engineering as a legitimate discipline. "When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing," she told El Pais in 2018. "It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline." Hamilton received numerous honors, including the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003, the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017, the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019, and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022. In 2015, the Apollo software she helped develop was added in its entirety to GitHub. In 2017, she became an official Lego Minifigure as part of the Women of NASA set, originally designed by MIT science communicator Maia Weinstock. "Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. "She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from." Hamilton is survived by her daughter, Lauren Hamilton; her son-in-law, Richard Selesnick; two grandsons; and four great-grandchildren. A memorial service will take place in the spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts. "When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing," she told El Pais in 2018. "It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. The Apollo software's architecture became a defining part of Hamilton's contribution to the program.MIT aerospace professor and interim department head Olivier de Weck described Hamilton as a major contributor to Apollo's success and to the development of software engineering.

She said the team developed new solutions while working with technology that was still poorly understood."From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009.
"To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement.
Hamilton described the software work as an unusually demanding experience because the missions allowed no second chance.
Hamilton applied for the work and became the first programmer on the Apollo project.Hamilton received numerous honors during her career, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom.
MIT said Hamilton worked at the institution from 1959 until the mid-1970s and later became a computing entrepreneur and CEO.The cause of her death was not disclosed, according to CNN.

Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936 and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics with a minor in philosophy from Earlham College in 1958.She moved to Boston in 1959 and began her computing career at MIT.

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, the MIT computing pioneer who led software development for NASA's Apollo program, died September 30 at age 90, according to MIT. Her work helped create the onboard software that guided crewed Apollo missions and helped establish software engineering as a professional discipline. MIT said Hamilton worked at the institution from 1959 until the mid-1970s and later became a computing entrepreneur and CEO.The cause of her death was not disclosed, according to CNN. Hamilton joined MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory after earlier programming work in meteorology and at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, where she worked on the SAGE air defense project. Her interest in software reliability grew during that period, according to MIT News.In 1965, Hamilton joined the Apollo effort after the Instrumentation Laboratory had won a NASA contract to develop onboard flight software. She became the first programmer hired for the Apollo project and later led teams responsible for software on crewed missions.By 1968, Hamilton was assistant director overseeing the Command and Service Module team, while more than 400 people worked on Apollo software, according to MIT News. CNN reported that she ultimately led a team of about 100 engineers designing software to guide NASA's Apollo missions. Hamilton described the software work as an unusually demanding experience because the missions allowed no second chance. She said the team developed new solutions while working with technology that was still poorly understood."From my own perspective, the software experience itself (designing it, developing it, evolving it, watching it perform and learning from it for future systems) was at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. Her work included developing approaches to software reliability and defensive programming, according to MIT News. The Apollo software's architecture became a defining part of Hamilton's contribution to the program.MIT aerospace professor and interim department head Olivier de Weck described Hamilton as a major contributor to Apollo's success and to the development of software engineering. "To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics.Hamilton's influence extended beyond Apollo. MIT said she authored more than 130 publications and continued working in systems software after leaving the university.Her achievements received national recognition in 2016, when President Barack Obama presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The White House citation credited her with advancing software engineering and helping make the Apollo lunar missions possible."Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon," the Presidential Medal of Freedom citation said. Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936 and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics with a minor in philosophy from Earlham College in 1958.She moved to Boston in 1959 and began her computing career at MIT. MIT News said Hamilton's first programming work involved weather prediction with meteorologist Edward N. Lorenz.She later joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1961 before moving to the Instrumentation Laboratory and the Apollo program.The NASA contract had sought programmers to develop software to "send man to the moon," according to MIT News. Hamilton applied for the work and became the first programmer on the Apollo project.Hamilton received numerous honors during her career, including the 2016 Presidential Medal of Freedom.

coreStoryFacts.text: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft.
When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.
Margaret Hamilton, the MIT computer scientist who led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept.
Her work helped land humans on the moon and established software engineering as a formal discipline.

"Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics.
Hamilton added a warning to the technical documentation and proposed a software fix to prevent the error during a real mission.
Her proposal was overruled on the grounds that trained astronauts would never make that mistake.
During the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during flight, wiping out the onboard navigational data.
Hamilton's team was called in to solve the error, and her proposed changes were then integrated into the program.
This became an early example of "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own.
Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised a 1202 alarm: the system was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch.
Houston trusted the software and allowed the mission to proceed.
Hamilton applied and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, and the first female programmer on the project.
By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, overseeing more than 400 people.

One incident, known as "the Lauren error," occurred when her four-year-old daughter Lauren accidentally activated a pre-launch program called P01 while playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab, crashing the simulator midflight.
"Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful," said Jerry M.
In 2015, the Apollo software she helped develop was added in its entirety to GitHub.

Margaret Hamilton, the MIT computer scientist who led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept. 30. She was 90. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s, first at the Instrumentation Lab and later at Lincoln Laboratory. She authored more than 130 publications and helped establish software engineering as a dedicated field. In 2016, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history," the White House citation read. "Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics at the University of Michigan before transferring to Earlham College, where she earned a bachelor's degree in 1958. She moved to Boston in 1959 and found a temporary position in MIT's meteorology department, working with professor Edward N. Lorenz on weather prediction software. That work later informed Lorenz's pioneering research on chaos theory. In 1961, Hamilton joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory as a programmer on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system. She wrote software for the prototype AN/FSQ-7 computer, which the U.S. Air Force used to search for potentially unfriendly aircraft. During this period, she became interested in software reliability, a concept that was largely unexplored at the time. In 1965, Hamilton was preparing to pursue graduate studies when her husband saw a newspaper advertisement: MIT's Instrumentation Lab was seeking programmers to develop software to send a man to the moon. NASA had awarded the lab the contract to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program. Hamilton applied and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, and the first female programmer on the project. She initially worked on software for uncrewed Apollo missions, then moved up to lead the team developing onboard flight software for crewed missions. By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, overseeing more than 400 people. "There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s," Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. "Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers." Hamilton's approach to software development proved critical during the Apollo missions. One incident, known as "the Lauren error," occurred when her four-year-old daughter Lauren accidentally activated a pre-launch program called P01 while playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab, crashing the simulator midflight. Hamilton added a warning to the technical documentation and proposed a software fix to prevent the error during a real mission. Her proposal was overruled on the grounds that trained astronauts would never make that mistake. During the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during flight, wiping out the onboard navigational data. Hamilton's team was called in to solve the error, and her proposed changes were then integrated into the program. This became an early example of "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own. Hamilton's most famous contribution came during the Apollo 11 mission in July 1969. Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised a 1202 alarm: the system was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch. Hamilton and her team had engineered priority-driven software that could shut down unnecessary background tasks to prioritize mission-critical functions. Houston trusted the software and allowed the mission to proceed. Two men walked on the moon for the first time. Hamilton continued at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s. As the Apollo program wound down, the lab spun out of MIT to become Draper Laboratory. "Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful," said Jerry M. Wohletz, president and CEO at Draper. "Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home." In 1976, Hamilton founded Higher Order Software, based on her approach of error prevention and fault tolerance. A decade later, she founded Hamilton Technologies, whose flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language for engineering complex software systems. Throughout her career, Hamilton fought for recognition of software engineering as a legitimate discipline. "When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing," she told El Pais in 2018. "It was an ongoing joke for a long time. They liked to kid me about my radical ideas. Software eventually and necessarily gained the same respect as any other discipline." Hamilton received numerous honors, including the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003, the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017, the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019, and induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022. "Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. "She personified leadership by example, and established a practice of software engineering based on problem-solving and systems engineering that we all benefit from." facts.text: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft.
When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.
Margaret Hamilton, the MIT computer scientist who led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept.
Her work helped land humans on the moon and established software engineering as a formal discipline.

"Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics.
Hamilton added a warning to the technical documentation and proposed a software fix to prevent the error during a real mission.
Her proposal was overruled on the grounds that trained astronauts would never make that mistake.
During the Apollo 8 mission in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently launched P01 during flight, wiping out the onboard navigational data.
Hamilton's team was called in to solve the error, and her proposed changes were then integrated into the program.
This became an early example of "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate or fix errors on its own.
Moments before the Eagle module was set to land on the lunar surface, the onboard computer raised a 1202 alarm: the system was overloaded due to a fault in a hardware switch.
Houston trusted the software and allowed the mission to proceed.
Hamilton applied and was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, and the first female programmer on the project.
By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, overseeing more than 400 people.

One incident, known as "the Lauren error," occurred when her four-year-old daughter Lauren accidentally activated a pre-launch program called P01 while playing with the command module simulator at the Instrumentation Lab, crashing the simulator midflight.
"Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful," said Jerry M.

In 1976, Hamilton founded Higher Order Software, based on her approach of error prevention and fault tolerance.
A decade later, she founded Hamilton Technologies, whose flagship product is the Universal Systems Language (USL), a systems modeling language for engineering complex software systems.

Eliminations for the 15th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals begin at 10 a.m. CT Sunday at World Wide Technology Raceway, and with the NHRA Countdown to the Championship reaching its midpoint, the margin between being prepared and being ready to win has never been smaller. Sunday is the portal through which every championship contender must pass. It is where qualifying promise becomes race-day performance, where momentum takes shape and where teams that are prepared just enough can be outpaced by those that are fully ready to win. The 17th of 20 events in the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series season is also the third of six races in the Countdown to the Championship. By Sunday evening, the title picture in Top Fuel, Funny Car, Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle could look dramatically different. Points leader Shawn Langdon enters eliminations as the No. 1 qualifier in Top Fuel after a 3.679-second run at 339.87 mph. Langdon has won three consecutive races, including the first two events of the Countdown, and will open against eight-time world champion Tony Schumacher. Schumacher qualified 16th with a 3.842, making the opening pairing a meeting between one of the hottest drivers in the sport and the most successful Top Fuel driver in NHRA history. Langdon’s Kalitta Motorsports teammate and closest championship rival, Doug Kalitta, starts from the No. 10 position and draws No. 7 qualifier Shawn Reed, giving the championship rivals very different routes through the ladder. The depth of the Top Fuel field is evident throughout the opening round. No. 2 qualifier Antron Brown faces Clay Millican, while rookie Maddi Gordon, who qualified third with a 3.708 at 340.65 mph, races Will Smith. Tony Stewart meets Josh Hart in a six-versus-11 matchup, and Leah Pruett faces Kyle Wurtzel in the closest pairing of the round, separated by just .001-second in qualifying. Justin Ashley, one of the category’s strongest leavers, qualified 12th and faces No. 5 qualifier Billy Torrence, while Michigan runner-up Spencer Massey opens against Jasmine Salinas. Funny Car may offer the most consequential first-round matchup of the morning. Back-to-back world champion Austin Prock qualified fourth with a 3.882 and will face No. 13 qualifier Ron Capps. Prock is trying to regain ground in the championship, while Capps entered the weekend among the closest challengers to points leader Matt Hagan. One of those title contenders will be finished before the second round. Jack Beckman leads the field with a 3.866 at 332.59 mph and begins eliminations against Dale Creasy Jr. Alexis DeJoria, whose 3.882 at 334.65 mph held the top spot after Friday, qualified second and will race Bobby Bode. Hagan begins Sunday from the No. 3 position against Terry Haddock. The four-time world champion arrives with an 84-point lead after winning at Rockingham and has reached the final round at four consecutive events. Hagan is also the defending St. Louis winner, but Sunday’s ladder offers no guarantees in a category where the top eight qualifiers are separated by only .055-second. Jordan Vandergriff, second in the standings after winning the Countdown opener in Michigan, qualified seventh and faces Cruz Pedregon. J.R. Todd will race Blake Alexander, Chad Green draws Spencer Hyde and Daniel Wilkerson faces Dave Richards in a matchup separated by just .002-second. Pro Stock’s championship fight is even tighter, and the qualifying sheet reflects it. The quickest eight cars are separated by only .016-second, creating an opening round in which reaction times and execution could carry as much weight as qualifying position. Troy Coughlin Jr. earned the No. 1 position with a 6.473 at 211.69 mph and will face Chris Vang. Coughlin opened the Countdown with a victory in Michigan and now has another opportunity to move deeper into the championship conversation. Points leader Greg Stanfield qualified second, just .001-second behind Coughlin, and races Mason McGaha. Defending event winner Greg Anderson starts third against Kenny Delco, while Aaron Stanfield faces Deric Kramer. Two pairings near the center of the ladder could create significant title movement. No. 6 qualifier Eric Latino faces reigning world champion Dallas Glenn, who starts 11th, and No. 8 qualifier Cody Anderson races six-time world champion Erica Enders. Enders owns six St. Louis victories and qualified only .002-second behind Anderson. Matt Hartford, who entered the weekend second in points, opens against Stephen Bell, while Jeg Coughlin Jr. races Matt Latino. In Pro Stock Motorcycle , Gaige Herrera made the category’s loudest qualifying statement with a track-record 6.644 at 202.76 mph. The three-time defending St. Louis winner begins eliminations against Malcolm Phillips Jr. as he tries to erase the 64-point deficit separating him from championship leader and Vance & Hines teammate Richard Gadson. Gadson qualified seventh and immediately faces No. 8 qualifier Chase Van Sant. Only .013-second separated them in qualifying, giving the points leader a demanding opening assignment at a point in the season when every round carries growing championship weight. Matt Smith qualified second with a 6.663 at a track-record speed of 203.12 mph and races Geno Scali. Angie Smith starts fourth against Michigan finalist Marc Ingwersen, while Michigan winner John Hall faces Steve Johnson. Joey Gladstone, Ryan Oehler and Clayton Howey are also positioned to influence a tightly packed championship field. Beyond the Mission Foods Series, Sunday’s program also includes eliminations in the NHRA Lucas Oil Drag Racing Series, the JBS Equipment NHRA Pro Mod Drag Racing Series presented by Elite Motorsports and the Flexjet NHRA Factory Stock Showdown. Fans can take part in the SealMaster Track Walk and the special pre-race ceremonies introducing the drivers competing for a prestigious 75th-anniversary Diamond Wally. Following the final rounds, fans are invited to the winner’s circle celebration to congratulate the newest St. Louis champions. The day will also place NHRA in one of its biggest television windows of the season. Most FOX markets will air the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals from 4:30-6:30 p.m. ET following football, while select markets will receive the race from 2-4 p.m. ET leading directly into football coverage. Qualifying determined where each team will begin. Sunday will reveal which teams are truly ready to step through the portal and perform like champions. Pre-race ceremonies at 9 a.m. NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series eliminations begin at 10 a.m. Sunday, Oct. 4, FOX will televise two hours of final eliminations coverage at either 2 p.m. or 4:30 p.m. ET, depending on the market. 2025 EVENT WINNERS Doug Kalitta, Top Fuel; Matt Hagan, Funny Car; Greg Anderson, Pro Stock; and Gaige Herrera, Pro Stock Motorcycle.
