Hagan begins Sunday from the No. 3 position against Terry Haddock. The four-time world champion arrives with an 84-point lead after winning at Rockingham and has reached the final round at four consecutive events. Hagan is also the defending St. Louis winner, but Sunday’s ladder offers no guarantees in a category where the top eight qualifiers are separated by only .055-second.

Jordan Vandergriff, second in the standings after winning the Countdown opener in Michigan, qualified seventh and faces Cruz Pedregon. J.R. Todd will race Blake Alexander, Chad Green draws Spencer Hyde and Daniel Wilkerson faces Dave Richards in a matchup separated by just .002-second.

Pro Stock’s championship fight is even tighter, and the qualifying sheet reflects it. The quickest eight cars are separated by only .016-second, creating an opening round in which reaction times and execution could carry as much weight as qualifying position.

Troy Coughlin Jr. earned the No. 1 position with a 6.473 at 211.69 mph and will face Chris Vang. Coughlin opened the Countdown with a victory in Michigan and now has another opportunity to move deeper into the championship conversation.

Points leader Greg Stanfield qualified second, just .001-second behind Coughlin, and races Mason McGaha. Defending event winner Greg Anderson starts third against Kenny Delco, while Aaron Stanfield faces Deric Kramer.

Two pairings near the center of the ladder could create significant title movement. No. 6 qualifier Eric Latino faces reigning world champion Dallas Glenn, who starts 11th, and No. 8 qualifier Cody Anderson races six-time world champion Erica Enders. Enders owns six St. Louis victories and qualified only .002-second behind Anderson. Matt Hartford, who entered the weekend second in points, opens against Stephen Bell, while Jeg Coughlin Jr. races Matt Latino.

In Pro Stock Motorcycle , Gaige Herrera made the category’s loudest qualifying statement with a track-record 6.644 at 202.76 mph. The three-time defending St. Louis winner begins eliminations against Malcolm Phillips Jr. as he tries to erase the 64-point deficit separating him from championship leader and Vance & Hines teammate Richard Gadson.

Gadson qualified seventh and immediately faces No. 8 qualifier Chase Van Sant. Only .013-second separated them in qualifying, giving the points leader a demanding opening assignment at a point in the season when every round carries growing championship weight.

Matt Smith qualified second with a 6.663 at a track-record speed of 203.12 mph and races Geno Scali. Angie Smith starts fourth against Michigan finalist Marc Ingwersen, while Michigan winner John Hall faces Steve Johnson. Joey Gladstone, Ryan Oehler and Clayton Howey are also positioned to influence a tightly packed championship field.

Beyond the Mission Foods Series, Sunday’s program also includes eliminations in the NHRA Lucas Oil Drag Racing Series, the JBS Equipment NHRA Pro Mod Drag Racing Series presented by Elite Motorsports and the Flexjet NHRA Factory Stock Showdown.

Fans can take part in the SealMaster Track Walk and the special pre-race ceremonies introducing the drivers competing for a prestigious 75th-anniversary Diamond Wally. Following the final rounds, fans are invited to the winner’s circle celebration to congratulate the newest St. Louis champions.

The day will also place NHRA in one of its biggest television windows of the season. Most FOX markets will air the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals from 4:30-6:30 p.m. ET following football, while select markets will receive the race from 2-4 p.m. ET leading directly into football coverage.

He’s won the first two races of the Countdown to the Championship playoffs – again obliterating the record book along the way – and will try to make it three straight in the postseason and four straight wins overall with a triumph this weekend in St. Louis. Langdon and the Kalitta Motorsports team have been impressively workmanlike during their brilliant run this year, laying the groundwork for one incredible win after another in their 12,000-horsepower Kalitta Air dragster. It’s put Langdon in the points lead and with seven wins in 2026 during NHRA’s 75th anniversary team, Langdon and his team are putting together a historic performance, which would be furthered if the past world champion can claim his second career win at World Wide Technology Raceway. “The Kalitta Air guys do a great job – they triple check themselves and work together to be perfect,” Langdon said. “Brian (Crew Chief Brian Husen) strives for perfection. You have to be perfect in order to win races and championships, and what we’re doing so far this year is a testament to the guys who are bonding together and working hard. We keep our heads down and keep working hard for the next one. We’ll do the same for St. Louis.” Last season, Doug Kalitta (Top Fuel), Matt Hagan (Funny Car), Greg Anderson (Pro Stock) and Gaige Herrera (Pro Stock Motorcycle) each claimed wins, while this year’s coverage also includes qualifying at 6:30 p.m. ET on FS1 and 11 a.m. on Sunday. Langdon and teammate Kalitta have – for the time being – made it a two-horse race in Top Fuel. Langdon leads Kalitta by just 25 points, but third-place Tony Stewart is a whopping 155 points back of Langdon, showcasing just how dominant Langdon has been for the bulk of the year. The class remains filled with talent, including Antron Brown, Leah Pruett, rookie standout Maddi Gordon, Justin Ashley and Josh Hart, but Langdon and his group have been on a remarkable pace in 2026. Langdon has been driven by coming up just short in the championship chase in recent seasons, looking to stay just a step ahead of Kalitta as the reigning world champion is after a third world title in the past four seasons. “I think we all feed off one another and it’s just a good working environment. We all work well together,” Langdon said. “We had a couple years of finishing second, finishing second in the regular season, and it’s not a bad spot to be, but it definitely gives you something to strive for. This is a team that’s stuck together and all the hard work is paying dividends. “Racing guys like Doug brings out the best in you and it’s humbling to beat a driver of that caliber. As good of a year as we’ve had, we’re only (25) points ahead of Doug, so there’s a lot of racing left.” Friday opens with two qualifying sessions, including a spectacular night session that includes the inaugural “Top Dog” competition presented by USEDHOTDOGS.com , as NHRA’s quickest qualifiers battle for $7,500 in bonus money. The NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals will also feature action in the NHRA Lucas Oil Drag Racing Series, the JBS Equipment NHRA Pro Mod Drag Racing Series presented by Elite Motorsports and Flexjet NHRA Factory Stock Showdown. Fans can enjoy the special pre-race ceremonies that introduce and celebrate each driver racing for the prestigious Wally on Sunday and includes the fan favorite SealMaster Track Walk, as well as the winner’s circle celebration on Sunday after racing concludes, where fans are invited to congratulate the St. Louis event winners. As always, fans get a pit pass to the most powerful and sensory-filled motorsports attraction. Fans can see their favorite teams in action and servicing their cars between rounds, get autographs from their favorite drivers and more. They can also visit NHRA’s Manufacturers Midway, which includes interactive displays, merchandise, food and fun. NHRA Mission Food Drag Racing Series qualifying will feature two rounds at 4:30 and 7 p.m. CT on Friday, Oct. 2, and the final two rounds on Saturday, Oct. 3 at 12 and 2:30 p.m. Final eliminations are scheduled for 10 a.m. CT on Sunday, Oct. 4. NHRA also offers the NHRA Jr. Street® program for teens and the Summit Racing Jr. Drag Racing League® for youth ages 5 to 17. With more than 100 Member Tracks, NHRA allows racers to compete at a variety of locations nationally and internationally. Eliminations for the 15th annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals begin at 10 a.m. CT Sunday at World Wide Technology Raceway, and with the NHRA Countdown to the Championship reaching its midpoint, the margin between being prepared and being ready to win has never been smaller. Sunday is the portal through which every championship contender must pass. It is where qualifying promise becomes race-day performance, where momentum takes shape and where teams that are prepared just enough can be outpaced by those that are fully ready to win. The 17th of 20 events in the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series season is also the third of six races in the Countdown to the Championship. By Sunday evening, the title picture in Top Fuel, Funny Car, Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle could look dramatically different. Points leader Shawn Langdon enters eliminations as the No. 1 qualifier in Top Fuel after a 3.679-second run at 339.87 mph. Langdon has won three consecutive races, including the first two events of the Countdown, and will open against eight-time world champion Tony Schumacher. Schumacher qualified 16th with a 3.842, making the opening pairing a meeting between one of the hottest drivers in the sport and the most successful Top Fuel driver in NHRA history. Langdon’s Kalitta Motorsports teammate and closest championship rival, Doug Kalitta, starts from the No. 10 position and draws No. 7 qualifier Shawn Reed, giving the championship rivals very different routes through the ladder. The depth of the Top Fuel field is evident throughout the opening round. No. 2 qualifier Antron Brown faces Clay Millican, while rookie Maddi Gordon, who qualified third with a 3.708 at 340.65 mph, races Will Smith. Tony Stewart meets Josh Hart in a six-versus-11 matchup, and Leah Pruett faces Kyle Wurtzel in the closest pairing of the round, separated by just .001-second in qualifying. Justin Ashley, one of the category’s strongest leavers, qualified 12th and faces No. 5 qualifier Billy Torrence, while Michigan runner-up Spencer Massey opens against Jasmine Salinas. Funny Car may offer the most consequential first-round matchup of the morning. Back-to-back world champion Austin Prock qualified fourth with a 3.882 and will face No. 13 qualifier Ron Capps. Prock is trying to regain ground in the championship, while Capps entered the weekend among the closest challengers to points leader Matt Hagan. One of those title contenders will be finished before the second round. Jack Beckman leads the field with a 3.866 at 332.59 mph and begins eliminations against Dale Creasy Jr. Alexis DeJoria, whose 3.882 at 334.65 mph held the top spot after Friday, qualified second and will race Bobby Bode. Hagan begins Sunday from the No. 3 position against Terry Haddock. The four-time world champion arrives with an 84-point lead after winning at Rockingham and has reached the final round at four consecutive events. Hagan is also the defending St. Louis winner, but Sunday’s ladder offers no guarantees in a category where the top eight qualifiers are separated by only .055-second. Jordan Vandergriff, second in the standings after winning the Countdown opener in Michigan, qualified seventh and faces Cruz Pedregon. J.R. Todd will race Blake Alexander, Chad Green draws Spencer Hyde and Daniel Wilkerson faces Dave Richards in a matchup separated by just .002-second. Pro Stock’s championship fight is even tighter, and the qualifying sheet reflects it. The quickest eight cars are separated by only .016-second, creating an opening round in which reaction times and execution could carry as much weight as qualifying position. Troy Coughlin Jr. earned the No. 1 position with a 6.473 at 211.69 mph and will face Chris Vang. Coughlin opened the Countdown with a victory in Michigan and now has another opportunity to move deeper into the championship conversation. Points leader Greg Stanfield qualified second, just .001-second behind Coughlin, and races Mason McGaha. Defending event winner Greg Anderson starts third against Kenny Delco, while Aaron Stanfield faces Deric Kramer. Two pairings near the center of the ladder could create significant title movement. No. 6 qualifier Eric Latino faces reigning world champion Dallas Glenn, who starts 11th, and No. 8 qualifier Cody Anderson races six-time world champion Erica Enders. Enders owns six St. Louis victories and qualified only .002-second behind Anderson. Matt Hartford, who entered the weekend second in points, opens against Stephen Bell, while Jeg Coughlin Jr. races Matt Latino. In Pro Stock Motorcycle , Gaige Herrera made the category’s loudest qualifying statement with a track-record 6.644 at 202.76 mph. The three-time defending St. Louis winner begins eliminations against Malcolm Phillips Jr. as he tries to erase the 64-point deficit separating him from championship leader and Vance & Hines teammate Richard Gadson. Gadson qualified seventh and immediately faces No. 8 qualifier Chase Van Sant. Only .013-second separated them in qualifying, giving the points leader a demanding opening assignment at a point in the season when every round carries growing championship weight. Matt Smith qualified second with a 6.663 at a track-record speed of 203.12 mph and races Geno Scali. Angie Smith starts fourth against Michigan finalist Marc Ingwersen, while Michigan winner John Hall faces Steve Johnson. Joey Gladstone, Ryan Oehler and Clayton Howey are also positioned to influence a tightly packed championship field. Beyond the Mission Foods Series, Sunday’s program also includes eliminations in the NHRA Lucas Oil Drag Racing Series, the JBS Equipment NHRA Pro Mod Drag Racing Series presented by Elite Motorsports and the Flexjet NHRA Factory Stock Showdown. Fans can take part in the SealMaster Track Walk and the special pre-race ceremonies introducing the drivers competing for a prestigious 75th-anniversary Diamond Wally. Following the final rounds, fans are invited to the winner’s circle celebration to congratulate the newest St. Louis champions. The day will also place NHRA in one of its biggest television windows of the season. Most FOX markets will air the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals from 4:30-6:30 p.m. ET following football, while select markets will receive the race from 2-4 p.m. ET leading directly into football coverage. Qualifying determined where each team will begin. Sunday will reveal which teams are truly ready to step through the portal and perform like champions. Race Photos from Sunday Eliminations – Final and Winner Circle Race Photos from Sunday Eliminations – Round 1 Shawn Langdon remains the hottest driver in NHRA competition, earning his fourth consecutive victory and eighth win of the 2026 season. The triumph also gives him wins in the opening three events of the six-race Countdown to the Championship playoffs. The No. 1 qualifier powered his dragster to a winning run of 3.732 seconds at 335.90 mph in the final round, defeating Will Smith, whose run was hampered by tire smoke early in the pass. The victory keeps Langdon undefeated at the midway point of the Countdown. “We’ve been good when we needed to be good, but we’ve been great when we needed to be great,” said Langdon. “Every time I hit the gas, I know I’m going to have a really dang good race car. Hopefully I don’t mess that up.” Langdon’s path to victory included wins over Tony Schumacher, Leah Pruett, Justin Ashley, and Smith, securing the 30th victory of his career. “At the beginning of the year, we had some goals in mind for our team, said Langdon. “We’ve been so close the last couple of years [winning a season championship]. We had the equipment, we had the personnel, we had the team to compete for championships, but it just didn’t work in our favor.” His four-race winning streak has expanded his lead in the standings to 116 points over second-place Doug Kalitta, with only three races remaining in the season. The weekend was even more impressive considering that Langdon set a new World Wide Technology Raceway speed record of 341.68 mph during the opening round of eliminations, eclipsing the mark established by Maddi Gordon just one day earlier. “I feel like I’m living a dream right now, but it’s a reality and it’s great to be a part of it,” said Langdon. Austin Prock made a powerful statement in Funny Car competition, reminding the field that he intends to defend his championship. To earn the victory, Prock navigated a challenging lineup that included Ron Capps, J.R. Todd, and No. 1 qualifier Jack Beckman before posting a winning run of 3.909 seconds at 332.84 mph to defeat Jordan Vandergriff in the final round. “We had to run through a lot of hitters today,” said Prock. “Each round was like a final round. Everybody we beat was in front of us in the Countdown. It was an epic way to cap it off. You don’t have days like this very often. When you run through four hitters like that, that’s like winning two races in one.” The victory moved Prock into third place in the Countdown standings, 106 points behind leader Matt Hagan with three races left on the schedule. “This was a big win. For the points, for our family, for our team — this is the time to get hot,” Prock said. “After everything we’ve been through this year, all the hours we haven’t slept and seven days a week working at this, it really pays off when you get a win.” The Pro Stock final featured a memorable father-versus-son showdown between Greg Stanfield and Aaron Stanfield. The elder Stanfield entered the matchup with a commanding 6-1 advantage in head-to-head competition and had previously won their only final-round meeting. However, Aaron turned the tables in St. Louis, winning on a holeshot thanks to a stellar .018-second reaction time. His 6.556-second pass at 209.20 mph narrowly defeated Greg’s .028 reaction time and quicker 6.547-second run at 209.85 mph. “It’s hard to get to the final round alone, and to be able to share it with my dad is pretty special. He’s taught me absolutely everything I know in a race car. I told him I was fixing to show him what he taught me,” Aaron said. “There were a lot of questions about whether we were going to race fair, and questions about if I laid down in the first round last weekend when he won. I think there are a lot of people who need to tip their hat right there. That final round shows what my dad and I are all about. We’re going to race as hard as we can possibly race. A thousandth at the stripe — it doesn’t get any better than that.” Aaron reached the final by defeating Deric Kramer, Matt Hartford, and Troy Coughlin Jr. The win was the 17th of his career and moved him into seventh place in the Countdown standings. “I don’t know what kind of shot I have at winning a championship, but I sure would like to see my dad win won.” said Aaron Stanfield. “He’s fought his whole career for this opportunity. I had to beg him to get back in a Pro Stock car, and obviously he’s still got a lot left in the tank.” Despite the runner-up finish, Greg Stanfield increased his Countdown lead to 71 points over Dallas Green. Gaige Herrera continued his remarkable success at World Wide Technology Raceway, capturing his fourth consecutive victory at the facility. Riding for the Vance & Hines Suzuki team, Herrera faced teammate and Countdown leader Richard Gadson in the final round. “Racing Richard in the final puts a lot of pressure on me,” said Herrera. “He’s the man on the tree. He’s very consistent, and it was awesome to race him in the final.” The victory moved Herrera within 32 points of Gadson in the battle for the season championship. “I felt like I was trying to push myself too much the last couple races,” said Herrera. “This whole weekend, I just reminded myself: I’m living the dream, I’m having fun and that’s what it’s all about.”

For 2026, Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (GOOGL) now projects that it will lay out between $175 billion and $185 billion on capital expenditures -- nearly double the amount it spent on them in 2025. That massive budget, which will largely go toward data centers, networking equipment, AI processors, and servers, is meant to keep the tech giant at the front of the pack in the increasingly expensive artificial intelligence (AI) race. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » But is this extensive infrastructure buildout a strategic masterstroke or a big mistake? The tech world is full of examples of companies that don't adapt to innovation quickly enough. Kodak had the chance to get into digital cameras early, but failed to. BlackBerry dismissed touchscreens. Blockbuster didn't take video streaming seriously. Executives are well aware of those history lessons and want to avoid having their businesses become case studies of what happens when a company doesn't adjust in time. If the value that AI winds up delivering lives up to the hype, Alphabet will have a solid foothold in that market that it will be able to enhance as it makes more investments. It has the chips and cloud services other companies need for the AI buildout, with its cloud division in particular offering a bright spot. In Q4 2025, Google Cloud revenue increased 48% year over year to $17.6 billion, and the segment's operating income increased 30.1% to $5.3 billion. Another proof point for Alphabet's cloud strength for AI use can be found in its backlog. "Google Cloud's backlog increased 55% sequentially and more than doubled year over year, reaching $240 billion at the end of the fourth quarter," said CFO Anat Ashkenazi on the company's Q4 earnings call. "The increase in backlog was driven by strong demand for our cloud products, led by our enterprise AI offerings, from multiple customers." It also has its own in-house products that it can optimize and monetize using AI, such as Google Search . Whenever you invest in a company, it's exciting to think about what can go right, but what's equally important, if not more so, is considering what can go wrong. There are several risks that come with Alphabet's impressive spending plans. One is that Wall Street may not have the patience to let the narrative fully play out before reaching a verdict on the stock. For example, Alphabet delivered what was generally considered a strong Q4 report, beating consensus top and bottom-line expectations. The stock price still took a hit, however, as management announced the scale of its 2026 capital expenditure plans. On Feb. 4, the day of the earnings announcement, Alphabet's Class A shares opened at $342.96. The next day, they opened 9% lower at at $312.09. That shows how much short-term concern can weigh down the stock price, but the biggest risk for the tech giant is that demand for AI processing power might not live up to expectations in the long term. If AI demand isn't at the levels expected for all the big tech players building out the infrastructure, the fears that they have been overspending could prove prophetic. As one of the companies with one of the biggest spending plans, Alphabet could be hit especially hard. Since the AI race started, Alphabet has been in a precarious position. One of the narratives early in the AI race was that Alphabet was caught flat-footed by OpenAI's launch of ChatGPT. Alphabet shifted that perception last year, and its shares rebounded, climbing roughly 66%. For 2026, one predominant theme in the market is worry that tech giants are spending too much on AI infrastructure when they may not reap strong enough returns on those investments. To separate the noise from what matters in this case, it helps to consider Alphabet's financial situation. It isn't a risky start-up going all-in on a speculative technology that will either make it or break it. It's generating huge profits in the here and now, with net income of $132 billion in 2025, a 32% increase from 2024. It also has diverse revenue sources and a bankroll that should allow it to navigate any setbacks and stumbles it encounters. Overall, whether you believe Alphabet needs to ramp up its spending or cut back on it, this will still require more than a quarter-to-quarter mindset as we all watch to see how it plays out. Before you buy stock in Alphabet, consider this: The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Alphabet wasn't one of them. For 2026, Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (GOOGL) now projects that it will lay out between $175 billion and $185 billion on capital expenditures -- nearly double the amount it spent on them in 2025. That massive budget, which will largely go toward data centers, networking equipment, AI processors, and servers, is meant to keep the tech giant at the front of the pack in the increasingly expensive artificial intelligence (AI) race. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » But is this extensive infrastructure buildout a strategic masterstroke or a big mistake? The tech world is full of examples of companies that don't adapt to innovation quickly enough. Kodak had the chance to get into digital cameras early, but failed to. BlackBerry dismissed touchscreens. Blockbuster didn't take video streaming seriously. Executives are well aware of those history lessons and want to avoid having their businesses become case studies of what happens when a company doesn't adjust in time. If the value that AI winds up delivering lives up to the hype, Alphabet will have a solid foothold in that market that it will be able to enhance as it makes more investments. It has the chips and cloud services other companies need for the AI buildout, with its cloud division in particular offering a bright spot. In Q4 2025, Google Cloud revenue increased 48% year over year to $17.6 billion, and the segment's operating income increased 30.1% to $5.3 billion. Another proof point for Alphabet's cloud strength for AI use can be found in its backlog. "Google Cloud's backlog increased 55% sequentially and more than doubled year over year, reaching $240 billion at the end of the fourth quarter," said CFO Anat Ashkenazi on the company's Q4 earnings call. "The increase in backlog was driven by strong demand for our cloud products, led by our enterprise AI offerings, from multiple customers." It also has its own in-house products that it can optimize and monetize using AI, such as Google Search . Whenever you invest in a company, it's exciting to think about what can go right, but what's equally important, if not more so, is considering what can go wrong. There are several risks that come with Alphabet's impressive spending plans. One is that Wall Street may not have the patience to let the narrative fully play out before reaching a verdict on the stock. For example, Alphabet delivered what was generally considered a strong Q4 report, beating consensus top and bottom-line expectations. The stock price still took a hit, however, as management announced the scale of its 2026 capital expenditure plans. On Feb. 4, the day of the earnings announcement, Alphabet's Class A shares opened at $342.96. The next day, they opened 9% lower at at $312.09. That shows how much short-term concern can weigh down the stock price, but the biggest risk for the tech giant is that demand for AI processing power might not live up to expectations in the long term. If AI demand isn't at the levels expected for all the big tech players building out the infrastructure, the fears that they have been overspending could prove prophetic. As one of the companies with one of the biggest spending plans, Alphabet could be hit especially hard. Since the AI race started, Alphabet has been in a precarious position. One of the narratives early in the AI race was that Alphabet was caught flat-footed by OpenAI's launch of ChatGPT. Alphabet shifted that perception last year, and its shares rebounded, climbing roughly 66%. For 2026, one predominant theme in the market is worry that tech giants are spending too much on AI infrastructure when they may not reap strong enough returns on those investments. To separate the noise from what matters in this case, it helps to consider Alphabet's financial situation. It isn't a risky start-up going all-in on a speculative technology that will either make it or break it. It's generating huge profits in the here and now, with net income of $132 billion in 2025, a 32% increase from 2024. It also has diverse revenue sources and a bankroll that should allow it to navigate any setbacks and stumbles it encounters. Overall, whether you believe Alphabet needs to ramp up its spending or cut back on it, this will still require more than a quarter-to-quarter mindset as we all watch to see how it plays out. extraction.body: Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it. He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range. So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate. Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026. A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap. The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform. That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it. The accounting environment is part of the reason. Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose. A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold. That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under ASU 2023-08, in-scope crypto assets — Bitcoin included — must be measured at fair value at every reporting date, with gains and losses flowing through net income each quarter. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC. Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices. In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined. When BTC drops, Robinhood's trading volumes compress and its crypto transaction revenue contracts. This has been true since the company launched crypto trading.What is new is that the $25 million corporate Bitcoin position is now marked to market every quarter under ASU 2023-08. When Bitcoin prices fall, Robinhood's quarterly earnings will now reflect unrealized losses on its corporate BTC holding — in addition to the revenue contraction from lower trading volumes. When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum. Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk. Robinhood sits in a new category: an operating company whose revenue is already Bitcoin-correlated and whose balance sheet is now also Bitcoin-marked-to-market."Cryptocurrencies' high volatility and uncertain regulatory landscape are misaligned with the fundamental goals of treasury management — stability, liquidity, and capital preservation," David Krause, a finance professor at Marquette University, noted in a January 2026 research publication on corporate Bitcoin holdings. Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically. But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs. Corporate: Why the Numbers Look ConfusingRobinhood controls approximately $25 billion in crypto assets across approximately 1.7 million wallet addresses on 12 different blockchains. A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder. Those $25 billion in crypto assets spread across Robinhood's customer custody wallets belong entirely to Robinhood's customers — Robinhood holds the private keys, but the coins are not on Robinhood's own books.The $25 million corporate BTC purchase is a different category. It sits on Robinhood's own balance sheet, subject to FASB ASU 2023-08 quarterly fair-value measurement. The distinction matters for both accounting and risk: customer custody creates zero direct P&L exposure for Robinhood (it earns custody-related revenue from fees and services, not from BTC price movements). The corporate position creates direct earnings exposure every quarter.Bitcoin was trading near $83,360 at the time of the DAS Asia disclosure, per CoinDesk market data.Robinhood's Position in the Corporate Bitcoin LandscapeWith the purchase, Robinhood joins a cohort that has expanded dramatically since Strategy made its initial $250 million BTC purchase in August 2020. More than 170 publicly traded companies worldwide now hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets, with combined corporate holdings exceeding 1.2 million BTC — representing more than 6% of Bitcoin's hard-capped supply of 21 million coins.Strategy remains the dominant holder by orders of magnitude. At approximately 848,000 BTC, it accounts for roughly 69% of all corporate-held Bitcoin globally. MARA Holdings and other Bitcoin miners hold substantial secondary positions. Among traditional, non-Bitcoin-native operating companies, Robinhood joins Tesla and Block (the payments company founded by Jack Dorsey) in what analysts describe as symbolic or diversification allocations rather than primary treasury strategies.The corporate treasury trend has also been bolstered by the FASB accounting shift. More than 140 publicly traded companies had adopted Bitcoin treasury positions in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with corporate treasuries collectively adding roughly 62,000 BTC in that quarter.Robinhood has not disclosed a formal BTC accumulation policy, and Kerbrat's language — emphasizing conviction over capital deployment — signals the company is not attempting to replicate Strategy's leveraged, all-in approach.Why Robinhood Chain Makes This More Than SymbolicRobinhood's Bitcoin balance sheet purchase did not arrive in isolation. It follows 98 days after Robinhood Chain — the company's permissionless Ethereum Layer 2 network built on Arbitrum's Orbit stack — went live on mainnet on July 1, 2026. He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range.
So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate.
Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026.
A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap.

The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform.

That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it.
The accounting environment is part of the reason.
Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose.
A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold.

That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024.
Under ASU 2023-08, in-scope crypto assets — Bitcoin included — must be measured at fair value at every reporting date, with gains and losses flowing through net income each quarter.

Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC.

Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices.
In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined.
When BTC drops, Robinhood's trading volumes compress and its crypto transaction revenue contracts.
This has been true since the company launched crypto trading.What is new is that the $25 million corporate Bitcoin position is now marked to market every quarter under ASU 2023-08.
When Bitcoin prices fall, Robinhood's quarterly earnings will now reflect unrealized losses on its corporate BTC holding — in addition to the revenue contraction from lower trading volumes.

When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum.

Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk.

Robinhood sits in a new category: an operating company whose revenue is already Bitcoin-correlated and whose balance sheet is now also Bitcoin-marked-to-market."Cryptocurrencies' high volatility and uncertain regulatory landscape are misaligned with the fundamental goals of treasury management — stability, liquidity, and capital preservation," David Krause, a finance professor at Marquette University, noted in a January 2026 research publication on corporate Bitcoin holdings.

Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically.
But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs.
Corporate: Why the Numbers Look ConfusingRobinhood controls approximately $25 billion in crypto assets across approximately 1.7 million wallet addresses on 12 different blockchains.
A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder.

Those $25 billion in crypto assets spread across Robinhood's customer custody wallets belong entirely to Robinhood's customers — Robinhood holds the private keys, but the coins are not on Robinhood's own books.The $25 million corporate BTC purchase is a different category.
It sits on Robinhood's own balance sheet, subject to FASB ASU 2023-08 quarterly fair-value measurement.

He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range. So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate. Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026. A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap. The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform. That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it. The accounting environment is part of the reason. Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose. A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold. That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under ASU 2023-08, in-scope crypto assets — Bitcoin included — must be measured at fair value at every reporting date, with gains and losses flowing through net income each quarter. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC. Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices. In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined. When BTC drops, Robinhood's trading volumes compress and its crypto transaction revenue contracts. This has been true since the company launched crypto trading.What is new is that the $25 million corporate Bitcoin position is now marked to market every quarter under ASU 2023-08. When Bitcoin prices fall, Robinhood's quarterly earnings will now reflect unrealized losses on its corporate BTC holding — in addition to the revenue contraction from lower trading volumes. When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum. Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk. Robinhood sits in a new category: an operating company whose revenue is already Bitcoin-correlated and whose balance sheet is now also Bitcoin-marked-to-market."Cryptocurrencies' high volatility and uncertain regulatory landscape are misaligned with the fundamental goals of treasury management — stability, liquidity, and capital preservation," David Krause, a finance professor at Marquette University, noted in a January 2026 research publication on corporate Bitcoin holdings. Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically. He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range.
So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate.
Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026.
A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap.

The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform.

That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it.
The accounting environment is part of the reason.
Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose.
A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold.

That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024.
Under ASU 2023-08, in-scope crypto assets — Bitcoin included — must be measured at fair value at every reporting date, with gains and losses flowing through net income each quarter.

In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined.
When BTC drops, Robinhood's trading volumes compress and its crypto transaction revenue contracts.
This has been true since the company launched crypto trading.What is new is that the $25 million corporate Bitcoin position is now marked to market every quarter under ASU 2023-08.
When Bitcoin prices fall, Robinhood's quarterly earnings will now reflect unrealized losses on its corporate BTC holding — in addition to the revenue contraction from lower trading volumes.

When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum.

Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk.

coreFacts.text: The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform.

Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC.

When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum.
In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined.

Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it.

Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk.
A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder.
Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose.
But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs.
Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026.

The distinction matters for both accounting and risk: customer custody creates zero direct P&L exposure for Robinhood (it earns custody-related revenue from fees and services, not from BTC price movements).
MARA Holdings and other Bitcoin miners hold substantial secondary positions.

Among traditional, non-Bitcoin-native operating companies, Robinhood joins Tesla and Block (the payments company founded by Jack Dorsey) in what analysts describe as symbolic or diversification allocations rather than primary treasury strategies.The corporate treasury trend has also been bolstered by the FASB accounting shift.
Robinhood has added approximately $25 million worth of bitcoin to its corporate balance sheet, marking a significant step in its growing involvement in cryptocurrency.
This move, confirmed by Robinhood's senior VP Johann Kerbrat, reflects the company's deep commitment to bitcoin and the crypto ecosystem.
Robinhood continues to expand its crypto offerings, including launching an Ethereum-compatible network and tokenized stock products, indicating ongoing growth in its crypto business.

“Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion [range].
The move puts Robinhood among a growing cohort of public companies holding BTC as a treasury asset.
Nasdaq-listed Strategy MSTR $154.55 · Market Closed started this trend in 2020 and now its followed by more than 170 firms worldwide.
Current corporate holders include names such as Tesla, Block, MARA Holdings, CleanSpark, and Riot Platforms, which together account for well over 1.2 million BTC across their balance sheets.

passages: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware.
It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths .
It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique.

It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.
The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly.
Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise.
I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now.
The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.
The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage.
A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport.
But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away.
Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback .
And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced .
Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware.
Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special.
Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM :
The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way.
Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible.
Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing.
There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating.
I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real.
Some of the little touches I was able to glean:
Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results.

extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special. Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.
passages: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.

The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product.
Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo .

In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean:

You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix.

It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special.

Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.)

And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.)
Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM :

The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.

It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come):

The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate.

All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying:
The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information…
Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza

And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core?
Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change.
CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

“We can be so much more than that.” Teenage Engineering did not immediately return a request for comment.
